<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
A sequence $\{D_N\}_{N\geq 1}$  in $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z$ is called {\em  $\rho$-equidistributed in}\index{Equidistribution!$\rho$-equidistribution} $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z$ if 
\begin{equation}\label{e.rho-tiltedness}
\forall\xi_1,\xi_2\in\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z,\ \ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\#\{1\leq N\leq n: D_N(\alpha)=\xi_1 \}}{\#\{1\leq N\leq n: D_N(\alpha)=\xi_2 \}}=\rho(\xi_1,\xi_2).
\end{equation}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $\rho\equiv 1$, we say that $\{D_N\}_{N\geq 1}$ is  {\em equidistributed}.

\item If $\rho\not\equiv 1$, we say that $\{D_N\}_{N\geq 1}$ is  {\em tilted, with profile $\rho$}. \index{Tilt} \index{Tilt!tilt profile} \index{Equidistribution!tilt}


\item If $\rho(\xi_1,\xi_2)=\exp[t(\xi_1-\xi_2)]$ for $t\neq 0$, we say that 
$\{D_N\}_{N\geq 1}$ is  {\em exponentially tilted, with  tilt parameter $t$}. \index{Tilt!exponential} \index{Tilt!tilt parameter}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{t.char-of-equidist-seq}
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational of bounded type,  and let \eqref{e.even-cfe} be the {\em even} continued fraction expansion of $\beta:=2\alpha-1$. Then $D_N(\alpha)$ is equidistributed in $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z$ iff 
\begin{equation}\label{e.sgn-criterion}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n [\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{t.tilt-and-exp-tilt}
Suppose $\alpha$ is an irrational of bounded type and $x\in\mathbb T$.
If  the sequence $D_N(\alpha,x+I)$ is  tilted, then it is necessarily exponentially tilted. \index{Tilt!implies exponential tilt}
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{t.exp-tilted-exist}
For every $\eta\in\mathbb R$, there exists an irrational $\alpha$ of bounded type so that $\{D_N(\alpha)\}$ is exponentially tilted with tilt parameter 
 $\eta$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\normalfont
 Nakada's work \cite{Nakada-Keio}\index{Nakada theorem} implies directly that for every irrational $\alpha$ and for every $\eta\in\mathbb R$, there exist $x$ such that  $D_N(\alpha,x+I)$ is exponentially tilted with tilt parameter $\eta$, see \S\ref{s.dynamical-reduction}.  Theorem \ref{t.exp-tilted-exist} says that for some $\alpha$, we can take $x=0$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
Do there exist irrationals  so that $D_N(\alpha)$ is  $\rho$-tilted but not exponentially tilted? (By Theorem \ref{t.tilt-and-exp-tilt} such $\alpha$ are  of unbounded type.) Which  $\rho$ are possible?
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{t.exponential-tilt-HD}
Suppose $\alpha$ is an irrational of bounded type. There exist positive constants $c_1,c_2$ such that for all $\eta$ small enough, 
    $$
    1-c_1 \eta^2\leq \mathrm{HD}(\mathsf{T}_\eta(\alpha))\leq 1-c_2 \eta^2.
    $$
In particular, the set of $x\in\mathbb T$ such that $D_N(\alpha,x+I)$  is exponentially tilted has full Hausdorff dimension (and zero Lebesgue measure).
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{t.no-equidist-no-tilt}
The set of $x\in\mathbb T$ such that $D_N(\alpha,x+I)$ is not  tilted and not equidistributed is a residual set with full Hausdorff dimension and zero Lebesgue measure.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{e.BU-thm}
Suppose $\alpha$ is an irrational of bounded type and ${\ell}\in (0,1)$ is rational, or more generally a real number in $(0,1)$ such that 
$$
\exists C>0\textrm{ s.t. }|q\alpha-\ell-p|>C/{|q|}\textrm{ for all }p\in\mathbb Z, q\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}\textrm{ s.t. }\gcd(p,q)=1.
$$
Then there exist $A_n\in\mathbb R$ and $B_n>0$ such that for all $a<b$,
$$
\frac{1}{n}\#\left\{1\leq N\leq n: \frac{D_N(\alpha,[0,\ell])-A_n}{B_n}\in [a,b]\right\}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_a^b e^{-t^2/2}dt.
$$
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{t.A_n-B_n-estimates}
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational of bounded type. Then there exist $A_n=O(\log n)$ and $B_n\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{e.Beck-A_n-B_n-TDLT}
\frac{1}{n}\#\left\{1\leq N\leq n: \frac{D_N(\alpha)-A_n}{B_n}\in [a,b]\right\}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_a^b e^{-t^2/2}dt.
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{t.A_n}
Let $\alpha$ be an irrational of bounded type, and expand $\beta=2\alpha-1$ into its {\em even} continued fraction expansion $\beta=[2m_0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$. Then one can choose the sequence $A_n$ in Theorem \ref{t.A_n-B_n-estimates} to be of the form 
$
\displaystyle A_n:=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{\nu_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]$, where $\nu_n$ is a non-decreasing sequence with bounded jumps, and $\nu_n\asymp\log n.$
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{c.A_n-zero-crit} 
Suppose $\alpha$ has bounded type, and $\beta=2\alpha-1$ has even continued fraction expansion $[2m_0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item {\em No Global Bias:} Theorem \ref{t.A_n-B_n-estimates} holds with $A_n=0$;
\item  $\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
If \eqref{e.Beck-A_n-B_n-TDLT} holds with two sequences $A_n,A_n'$, then  $\displaystyle \frac{|A_n-A_n'|}{\sqrt{\log n}}\asymp \frac{|A_n-A_n'|}{B_n}\to 0$. Thus \eqref{e.Beck-A_n-B_n-TDLT} holds with $A_n=0$ iff 
$\displaystyle 
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\log n}}\sum_{j=1}^{\nu_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\to 0$, with $\nu_n$ as in Theorem \ref{t.A_n}. 
This is equivalent to $
\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu_n}}\sum_{j=1}^{\nu_n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\to 0
$, 
since $\nu_n\asymp \log n$, and to $
\displaystyle  \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\to 0
$, 
since $0\leq \nu_{n+1}-\nu_n\leq \operatorname{const}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{c.GB-LB} 
For quadratic irrationals, (LB)$\Leftrightarrow$(GB). For irrationals of bounded type, (LB)$\Rightarrow$(GB) but (GB)$\not\Rightarrow$(LB).
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By the previous results,   (LB) 
$\displaystyle \Leftrightarrow\frac{1}{{n}} \sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\not\to 0$,  and 
(GB) $\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\not\to 0$.  Thus, (LB)$\Rightarrow$(GB). 

To see that  (GB)$\not\Rightarrow$(LB), take $\alpha:=\frac{1}{2}(\beta+1)$ where 
$
\beta:=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots,] 
$, $m_i$ is a bounded sequence in $\mathbb Z\setminus\{0,1\}$, and 
$\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\sim n^{2/3}$.  By Lemma~\ref{l.BT-bounded-pm-two},  $\beta$ has bounded type, and therefore $\beta$ is  badly approximable by rationals. Thus $\alpha$ is badly approximable by rationals, and $\alpha$ has bounded type. By Theorem \ref{t.char-of-equidist-seq},  $D_N(\alpha)$ is equidistributed, and (LB) fails. But by  Corollary \ref{c.A_n-zero-crit}, (GB) holds. 

Now suppose that $\alpha$ is a quadratic irrational. Then $\beta$  is a quadratic irrational,   the {\em even} CFE of $\beta$ is eventually periodic \cite{Kraaikamp-Lopes},\index{Kraaikamp-Lopes theorem}\index{Even continued fraction expansion!of quadratic irrationals} and $$\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]= \operatorname{const} n+O(1).$$ If the constant is zero, (GB) and (LB) both fail. If the constant is non-zero, (GB) and (LB) both hold. So for quadratic irrationals,  (GB)$\Leftrightarrow$(LB).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{t.LLT-for-D_N}
For every  irrational  $\alpha$ of bounded type there are constants $A_n=O(\log n)$ as in Theorem \ref{t.A_n}, and $B_n\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$ as follows: If $\xi_n\in\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z$, $t\in\mathbb R$, and $\displaystyle \frac{\xi_n-A_n}{B_n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}t$, then 
$
\displaystyle\#\left\{1\leq N\leq n: D_N(\alpha)=\xi_n\right\}=[1+o(1)]
\frac{ne^{-t^2/2}}{\sqrt{8\pi B_n^2}}\textrm{ as }n\to\infty.
$
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{c.LLT-for-D_N}
Suppose $\alpha$ is an irrational of bounded type, and $\beta:=2\alpha-1$ has even CFE $[2m_0;2m_1,\ldots]$. If  $\displaystyle \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2j-1})]\to 0$, then
$$
\forall \xi\in\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z,\quad
  \#\left\{1\leq N\leq n: D_N(\alpha)=\xi\right\}\asymp n/\sqrt{\log n}.
 $$
 If, in addition, $\alpha$ is a quadratic irrational, then there is a positive constant such that
 $$
\forall \xi\in\frac{1}{2}\mathbb Z,\quad
  \#\left\{1\leq N\leq n: D_N(\alpha)=\xi\right\}\sim\operatorname{const} n/\sqrt{\log n}.
 $$
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The first statement follows directly from Theorem \ref{t.LLT-for-D_N}; the second is because in the case of quadratic irrationals, $B_n/\sqrt{\log n}\to $positive constant, by Beck's theorem \cite{Beck-Giant-Leap-1,Beck-Giant-Leap-2} (for a short dynamical proof, see \cite{Avila-Dolgopyat-Duryev-Sarig}).
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{t.ANSS} If $\alpha\not\in\mathbb Q$, then  every ergodic $T_\alpha$-invariant Borel measure on $\mathbb T\times\mathbb Z$ which assigns finite measure to every compact set  is proportional to  $\nu_t$ for some $t\in\mathbb R$.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
\label{d.generic}
A point $x_0\in X$ is called {\em $\mu$-generic}\index{Generic points} for  $T$ (resp. $\varphi$), if for any pair of non-negative $h_1,h_2\in C_c(X)$ such that $\mu(h_2)\neq 0$, 
$$
\frac{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h_1(T^j x_0)}{\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} h_2(T^j x_0)}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\frac{\mu(h_1)}{\mu(h_2)},\ 
\left(\textrm{resp. }
\frac{\int_0^{T} h_1(\varphi^t x_0)dt}{\int_{0}^{T} h_2(\varphi^t x_0)dt}\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}\frac{\mu(h_1)}{\mu(h_2)}
\right).
$$
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{t.HHW}\index{Hooper-Hubert-Weiss theorem}\index{Infinite staircase!and the cylinder map}\index{Cylinder map!and the infinite staircase}\index{Linear flow!Poincar\'e section for}
$\displaystyle \Sigma:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}($the top side of ${\mathsf{R}}_k)$  is a Poincar\'e section for $\phi$. The roof function is constant, equal to $1$. The Poincar\'e map is conjugate to the cylinder map $T_\alpha$, via the conjugacy  
$$
\omega:\mathbb T\times\mathbb Z\to\Sigma,\ \omega(x,k):=\left(\begin{array}{l}
\textrm{the point on the top side of ${\mathsf{R}}_k$, $y$ distance units right}\\
\textrm{of the middle, where $y\in [-1,1)$, $y=2x\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2$.}
   
                                                                 
                                                           
\end{array}\right).
$$
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- cor-4: body_md -->
\label{c.HHW}\index{Invariant Radon measures!$\mu_\xi$}
\label{c.Maharam-Measures} For every $\xi\in\mathbb R$ there is a unique locally finite ergodic $\phi$-invariant measure $\mu_{\xi}$ such that $\mu_\xi\circ D=e^{\xi}\mu_\xi$, and $\mu_\xi({\mathsf{R}}_0)=1$. For $\xi=0$,  $\mu_0=\frac{1}{2}\times$area measure. Any locally finite $\phi$-invariant and ergodic measure is proportional to  $\mu_\xi$ for some $\xi$.
<!-- end cor-4 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{Prop-Automorphisms}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  For every $A\in\Gamma(2)$ there exists a unique homogeneous automorphism $\widetilde{\psi}$  with $d\widetilde{\psi}=A$ and $\delta(\widetilde{\psi})=0$. This automorphism fixes the singularities.

\item  There is also a homogeneous automorphism with drift $\frac{1}{2}$ and derivative ${\tiny \biggl(\begin{array}{cc}
0 & -1\\
1 & 0
\end{array}\biggr)}$.

\item  Every homogeneous automorphism of ${\mathsf{St}}$ is a product of homeomorphisms from parts (1) and (2). 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- thm-12: body_md -->
\label{CrLebGen} 
Suppose ${\widetilde{\omega}}\in{\mathsf{St}}$. 
The following are equivalent:
(a) ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is $\mu_0$-generic;
(b) $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})}{n}=0$;
(c) $\displaystyle \forall k,\ell\in\mathbb Z,\ \lim_{T\to \infty} \frac{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{R}}_k} (\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt}
{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{R}}_\ell} (\phi^t ({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt}=1$.
<!-- end thm-12 -->
<!-- cor-5: body_md -->
\label{CrCEqui}
$D_N(\alpha,x+I)$ is equidistributed iff $\displaystyle\lim\limits_{N\to\infty}{z_n({\widetilde{\omega}}(-x,0))}/{n}=0$.
<!-- end cor-5 -->
<!-- cor-6: body_md -->
\label{CrOrigin} 

${\widetilde{\omega}}_0:=$the midpoint of the top side of ${\mathsf{R}}_0$ is $\mu_0$-generic iff 
\begin{equation}
\label{SignChanges}
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k-1})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k})\right]=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end cor-6 -->
<!-- thm-13: body_md -->
\label{CrLebGen2} 
Suppose ${\widetilde{\omega}}\in{\mathsf{St}}$. 
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item[(a)] ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is $\mu_0$-generic;
\item[(b)] $\displaystyle \lim_{T\to \infty} \frac{\log \Big( \int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt\Big)}
{\log \Big(\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_+} (\phi^t ({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt\Big)}=1$, where  ${\mathsf{St}}_+:=\bigcup_{k\geq 0}{\mathsf{R}}_k$, ${\mathsf{St}}_-:=\bigcup_{k<0}{\mathsf{R}}_k$;
\item [(c)] $\displaystyle \lim_{T\to \infty} \left(\log  \int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{R}}_0} (\phi^t ({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt\right)\bigg/\log T=1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-13 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\normalfont
It is natural to wonder if the logarithms in condition (b)
 could be removed. A  related question is whether  $\mu_0$-generic orbits spend asymptotically half of their time in ${\mathsf{St}}_-$ and ${\mathsf{St}}_+$.  The answer to both these questions is {\em negative}. See Corollary~\ref{PrBalance} in 
  \S\ref{ss.Limit-Thms-Statements} below. \index{Generic points!for $\mu_0$}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- thm-14: body_md -->
\label{t.Char-mu-xi-Gen}
\label{ThGen} 
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item[(a)] ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is $\mu_\xi$-generic;
\item[(b)] $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} \xi_n({\widetilde{\omega}})=\xi$;
\item[(c)] $\displaystyle \forall k,\ell\in\mathbb Z,\ \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{R}}_k}(\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}))dt}{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{R}}_\ell}(\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}))dt}=e^{\xi(k-\ell)}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-14 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Our proof gives a stronger result: There is a constant $R$ such that 
if the limit in (c)  holds for all $k,\ell$ {\em in an interval of length $R$}, then ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is generic for some $\mu_\xi.$ Is it enough to assume that the limit in (c) holds just for $k=0,\ell=1$?
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- thm-15: body_md -->
\label{CrWeakBal}
For every $\eta\in\mathbb R$ there exists a $\beta$ of bounded type so that 
${\widetilde{\omega}}_0$, the midpoint of the top side of ${\mathsf{R}}_0$,  is $\mu_\eta$-generic for the linear flow $\varphi_{\vec{v}}$ with  velocity $\vec{v}={\beta\choose 1}$.
<!-- end thm-15 -->
<!-- thm-16: body_md -->
\label{CrHDGen}
There are  constants $c_1, c_2>0$ such that for small $\xi$, 
$$ 2-c_1 \xi^2\leq \mathrm{HD}(\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))\leq 2-c_2 \xi^2. $$
<!-- end thm-16 -->
<!-- thm-17: body_md -->
\label{CrHDExcept}
The set of points which are not generic for any locally finite ergodic invariant measure of $\phi$ is a 
residual set of Hausdorff
dimension 2 and zero Lebesgue measure.
<!-- end thm-17 -->
<!-- thm-18: body_md -->
\label{c.diff-xi-diff-asymp}
Suppose $\xi_1>\xi_2\geq 0$ or $\xi_1<\xi_2\leq0$, and let $h$ be a function in $L^1(\mu_{\xi_1})\cap L^1(\mu_{\xi_2})$ such that  $\int h d\mu_{\xi_i}>0$ $(i=1,2)$. Then 
for some $r>0$ independent of $h$, for  $(\mu_{\xi_1}\times\mu_{\xi_2})$-a.e. $({\widetilde{\omega}}_1,{\widetilde{\omega}}_2)$,
$\displaystyle
\frac{\int_0^T h(\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}_2))dt}{\int_0^T h(\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}_1))dt}>T^r\textrm{  for all $T$ large enough.} 
$
<!-- end thm-18 -->
<!-- thm-19: body_md -->
\label{CrDriftSeq}
For each $\xi$ there is a sequence $z_n^\xi$ (which depends on $\beta$) such that \index{Generic points!for $\mu_\xi$}
${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is $\mu_\xi$-generic  iff $\displaystyle \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})-z_n^\xi}{n}=0.$
<!-- end thm-19 -->
<!-- thm-20: body_md -->
\label{CrLogOTDetXi}
Suppose $\xi>0$, then: 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  
For some $0<c(\xi)<1$,  $c(\xi)\log T\leq \mathbb{I}_T^\xi\leq \log T$ for all $T$ large enough;
\item  If $\xi_1>\xi_2>0$, then $\displaystyle\liminf\limits_{T\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{I}_T^{\xi_2}-\mathbb{I}_T^{\xi_1}}{\log T}>0$;
\item
{If $\omega$ is generic for $\mu_\xi$ then} 
  $\displaystyle \lim_{T\to\infty}\!\! \frac{\mathbb{I}_T(\omega)-\mathbb{I}_T^\xi}{\log T}=0$;
\end{enumerate}
A similar result holds for $\xi<0$ and $\xi_1<\xi_2<0$, with $\{{\mathfrak{z}}\leq 1\}$
replaced by $\{{\mathfrak{z}}\geq -1\}.$
<!-- end thm-20 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
\label{d.historical}
 A locally finite Borel measure \index{Historical measures} $\mu$ on $X^\ast$ is called  {\em historical} for $x_0\in X$, if $\exists T_n\to\infty$ such that for any pair of functions $h_1,h_2\in C_c(X)$ such that $\int h_2 d\mu\neq 0$,
$$
\frac{\int_0^{T_n} h_1(\varphi^t(x_0))dt}{\int_0^{T_n} h_2(\varphi^t(x_0))dt}
\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\frac{\int h_1 d\mu}{\int h_2 d\mu}.
$$
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- thm-21: body_md -->
\label{t.historical-crit} Suppose ${\widetilde{\omega}}\in{\mathsf{St}}$ and $\xi_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$ is given by \eqref{e.xi-def}.
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\xi\in\mathbb R$ is a limit point of $\xi_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$
iff  $\mu_\xi$ is a historical measure of ${\widetilde{\omega}}$. 
\item If $\infty$ or $-\infty$ are limit points of $\xi_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$, then   there are two finite unions of horizontal rectangles $\mathsf F_1$, $\mathsf F_2$ and  a sequence $ T_n\to\infty$  such that 
$\displaystyle
\frac{\int_0^{T_n}1_{\mathsf F_1}(\varphi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}))dt}{\int_0^{T_n}1_{\mathsf F_2}(\varphi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}))dt}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.
$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-21 -->
<!-- thm-22: body_md -->
\label{CrHist}
For every ${\widetilde{\omega}}\in{\mathsf{St}}$, every historical measure is proportional  to $\mu_\xi$ for some $\xi$, and the set $\mathcal H({\widetilde{\omega}}):=\{\xi\in\mathbb R:\mu_\xi\textrm{ is historical for }{\widetilde{\omega}}\}$ is either empty, a singleton, or an interval (possibly infinite).
<!-- end thm-22 -->
<!-- thm-23: body_md -->
\label{ThStairTLT}
There are $\sigma_T$ and  $a_T({\widetilde{\omega}})$ 
such that for every ${\widetilde{\omega}}$,
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\displaystyle
\forall a<b,\ \lim\limits_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T} \mathrm{mes}\left\{t\in [0,T]:\frac{{\mathfrak{z}}(\phi^t {\widetilde{\omega}})\!-\!a_T({\widetilde{\omega}})}{\sigma_T}\in [a,b]\right\}=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_a^b e^{-s^2/2}ds
$;
\item 
For some $C$, for all ${\widetilde{\omega}}$, for all $T>C$, $|a_T({\widetilde{\omega}})|\leq C \log T$ and 
$C^{-1}\leq \frac{\sigma_T}{\sqrt{\log T}}\leq C$;


\item   For some $C$, for all ${\widetilde{\omega}}$, for all $T>C$, there is $n=n(T)\in\mathbb N$ so that   
$C^{-1}<\frac{n}{\log T}<C$, and $a_T({\widetilde{\omega}})=z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$,     see \eqref{e.z-n}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-23 -->
<!-- thm-24: body_md -->
\label{t.Local-TCLT} 
In the notation of the previous theorem, if $k_T\in\mathbb Z$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $\displaystyle\frac{k_T-a_T({\widetilde{\omega}})}{\sigma_T}\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{}s$, then
$$
\frac{1}{T}\mathrm{mes}\{t\in [0,T]: \phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}})\in{\mathsf{R}}_{k_T}\}=[1+o(1)]\frac{e^{-s^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_T^2}},\textrm{ as }T\to\infty.
$$
<!-- end thm-24 -->
<!-- thm-25: body_md -->
\label{PrBalance-second half}
For Lebesgue a.e. ${\widetilde{\omega}}$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, for all $T$ large enough,
$
\displaystyle \int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-}(\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}}))dt\geq \frac{T}{(\log\log T)^{1+\varepsilon}}
$. 
Moreover, the power is optimal:
\begin{equation}
\label{Bal3}
 \liminf_{T\to\infty} \frac{\log \left[\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t({\widetilde{\omega}})) dt\right]-\log T}{\log\log\log T}=-1\textrm{ Lebesgue a.e.}
  \end{equation}
A similar statement holds with ${\mathsf{St}}_+$ instead of ${\mathsf{St}}_-$.
<!-- end thm-25 -->
<!-- cor-7: body_md -->
For Lebesgue almost every point, 
\label{PrBalance}
  \begin{equation}
\label{Bal1}
 \liminf_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t{\widetilde{\omega}}) dt=0,
 \textrm{ whence }\liminf_{T\to \infty} \frac{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t{\widetilde{\omega}}) dt}
{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_+} (\phi^t {\widetilde{\omega}}) dt}=0.
 \end{equation}
 \begin{equation}
\label{Bal2}
\limsup_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{T}\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t{\widetilde{\omega}}) dt=1,  \textrm{ whence }\limsup_{T\to \infty} \frac{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-} (\phi^t{\widetilde{\omega}}) dt}
{\int_0^T 1_{{\mathsf{St}}_+} (\phi^t {\widetilde{\omega}}) dt}=\infty,
 \end{equation}
<!-- end cor-7 -->
<!-- thm-26: body_md -->
\label{ThLT-ZD}
There is a function $a_T\asymp T/\sqrt{\log T}$ such that if
${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is distributed on the staircase according to a smooth compactly supported probability density with respect to $\mu_0$, then for each
non-negative $h\in L^1(\mu_0)$ such that $\int h d\mu_0=1$, we have
$$
\frac{1}{a_T}\mathfrak I_T({\widetilde{\omega}},h)\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{dist}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal N^2\right),
\quad \textrm{and}\quad \frac{\mathfrak I_T({\widetilde{\omega}},1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-})}{T}\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{dist}\mathcal U.
$$
<!-- end thm-26 -->
<!-- thm-27: body_md -->
\label{ThLT-NZD}
For each $\xi>0$
there are functions $$a_T(\xi)\asymp\sqrt{\log T} \quad and \quad
(1-c)\log T\leq b_T(\xi)\leq \log T\quad with \quad 0<c<1$$ 
such that for every smooth compactly supported  probability density $\varphi$  with respect to $\mu_\xi$, if 
${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is distributed on the staircase according to $\varphi d\mu_\xi$, and $h\in L^1(\mu_\xi)$ is 
 non-negative with positive integral (e.g. $h=1_{{\mathsf{St}}_-}$), then
$$ \frac{\log \mathfrak{I}_T({\widetilde{\omega}}, h)-b_T(\xi) }{a_T(\xi) }\xrightarrow[T\to\infty]{\textrm{dist}}  \mathcal{N}.
$$
                                                                                                                            
The same result holds for $\xi<0$ with  ${\mathsf{St}}_+$ instead of ${\mathsf{St}}_-$.\index{Convergence in distribution}\index{Birkhoff integrals of the linear flow}
<!-- end thm-27 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
The following identities hold:
\begin{align}
   A_{k}(\beta)  &=
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         -2m_{2k} & 1 \\
         1 & 0 \\
       \end{array}
     \right)
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         -2m_{2k-1} & 1 \\
         1 & 0 \\
       \end{array}
     \right)\cdots
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         -2m_2 & 1 \\
         1 & 0 \\
       \end{array}
     \right)
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         -2m_1 & 1 \\
         1 & 0 \\
       \end{array}
     \right); \label{e.A-k-prime}\\
 A_{k}(\beta)&=
\left[\left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         0 & 1 \\
         1 & 2m_{1}\\
       \end{array}
     \right)
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         0 & 1 \\
         1 & 2m_{2} \\
       \end{array}
     \right)\cdots
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         0 & 1 \\
         1 & 2m_{2k-1} \\
       \end{array}
     \right)
     \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
         0 & 1 \\
         1 & 2m_{2k} \\
       \end{array}\right)\right]^{-1} \label{e.A-k-dagger} ;\\
 A_k(\beta)&= \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        p_{2k-1}  & p_{2k}  \\
         q_{2k-1} & q_{2k}  \\
       \end{array}\right)^{{-1}}\!\!\!\!,\textrm{ where }\frac{p_{j}}{q_{j}}=[0;2m_{1},\ldots,2m_{j}], \textrm{ and } (p_{j},q_{j})=1.
       \label{e.A-k-pq}
\end{align}
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
\eqref{e.A-k-prime} is because
$\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
1 & a \\
0 & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
1 & 0 \\
b & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right)=\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
ab+1 & a \\
b & 1 \\
\end{array}
\right)=\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
a & 1 \\
1 & 0 \\
\end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
b & 1 \\
1 & 0 \\
\end{array}
\right)
$. 
\eqref{e.A-k-dagger} follows from \eqref{e.A-k-prime} and the identity 
$ \left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & a \\
\end{array}
\right)^{-1}\!\!\!=\!\!\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
-a & 1 \\
1 & 0 \\
\end{array}
\right)$.  By  \cite[Ch.~1]{Khintchine-Continued-Fractions},  the reduced form $p_{k}/q_{k}$ of the fraction $[0;2m_1,\ldots,2m_{k}]$ is given recursively by 
$$
\left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        p_{k}  & p_{k+1}  \\
         q_{k} & q_{k+1}  \\
       \end{array}\right)=\left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        p_{k-1}  & p_{k}  \\
         q_{k-1} & q_{k}  \\
       \end{array}\right)\left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        0  & 1  \\
         1 & 2m_{k+1}  \\
       \end{array}\right)\ ;\  \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        p_{-1}  & p_{0}  \\
         q_{-1} & q_{0}  \\
       \end{array}\right)=
       \left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        1  & 0  \\
         0 & 1 \\
       \end{array}\right).
$$
The matrix product inside the square brackets in  \eqref{e.A-k-dagger} satisfies  the same recurrence. So $A_{k}(\beta)=\left(
       \begin{array}{cc}
        p_{2k-1}  & p_{2k}  \\
         q_{2k-1} & q_{2k}  \\
       \end{array}\right)^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{l.disonance}
Suppose $M<\infty$,
                                                
 and let $K$ be a compact subset of $(-1,1)$. Then there are constants $C>0, 0<\eta<1$ which only depend on $M$ and $K$ such that if $M(\beta)\leq M$, $\rho\in K$, $k\geq 1$, and $\beta=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$ where $m_i\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, then 
$$
\left\|\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_1 \\
\end{array}
\right)\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_2 \\
\end{array}
\right)\cdots
\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_k \\
\end{array}
\right){\rho\choose 1}\right\|\geq C^{-1}\eta^{-k}.
$$
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $B_k\!\!:=\!\!{\tiny \left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_1 \\
\end{array}
\right)\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_2 \\
\end{array}
\right)\cdots
\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & 2m_k \\
\end{array}
\right)}$. By \eqref{e.proj-action},
$$
{\widehat\sigma}\left[B_k{\tiny \left(
                   \begin{array}{c}
                     \rho \\
                     1 \\
                   \end{array}
                 \right)
}\right]=(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_k})(\rho).
$$
By Lemma \ref{l.v-contracts}, there exists $C>0$ and $0<\eta<1$ which only depend on $M$ such that $|(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_k})'|\leq C\eta^k$ on $[-1,1]$. It follows that for every $\rho,\rho'\in [-1,1]$,
\begin{equation}
\label{DeltaSigma}
\left|{\widehat\sigma}\left[B_k{\tiny \left(
                   \begin{array}{c}
                     \rho \\
                     1 \\
                   \end{array}
                 \right)
}\right]-{\widehat\sigma}\left[B_k{\tiny \left(
                   \begin{array}{c}
                     \rho' \\
                     1 \\
                   \end{array}
                 \right)
}\right]\right|\leq C\eta^k.
\end{equation}
Therefore, the angle between $B_k{\rho\choose 1}$ and $B_k{\rho'\choose 1}$ tends to zero uniformly exponentially fast as $k\to\infty$, whenever $\rho,\rho'\in (-1,1)$,

Now suppose $\rho\in K$, where $K$ is a compact subset of $(-1,1)$. Choose ${\varepsilon}_0$ so small that the closed  ${\varepsilon}_0$-neighborhood of $K$ is inside $(-1,1)$, and take $\rho':=\rho+{\varepsilon}_0$ and $\rho'':=\rho-{\varepsilon}_0$.
Let $Q$ denote the parallelogram generated by the vectors $\frac{1}{2}{\rho'\choose 1}$ and $\frac{1}{2}{\rho''\choose 1}$. Since $\det B_k=1$, the parallelogram $B_k(Q)$ has the same area as $Q$, but the angle between its generating vectors $B_k{\rho'\choose 1}, B_k{\rho''\choose 1}$ tends to zero uniformly exponentially as $k\to\infty$, at a rate which only depends on $M$.

 Necessarily, the length of the  principal diagonal $B_k{1\choose\rho}$ tends to infinity at an exponential rate, which only depends on $M$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{l.A-contracts}Suppose $M<\infty$, then there are $C>0$ and $0<\eta<1$ such that if $\beta\in (-1,1)\setminus\mathbb Q$ and $M(\beta)\leq M$, then 
$\|A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1}\|\leq C \eta^k$ for all $k\geq 0$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Write $\beta=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots,2m_{2k},r_{2k+1}]$, where $r_{2k+1}=[2m_{2k+1};2m_{2k+2},\ldots]$. 
 In the notation of the proof of the previous lemma,
$$
{\widehat\sigma}\left[{\beta\choose 1}\right]=\beta=(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_{2k}})
\left(\frac{1}{r_{2k+1}}\right)={\widehat\sigma}\left[B_k {1\choose r_{2k+1}}\right]={\widehat\sigma}\left[B_k {1/r_{2k+1}\choose 1}\right].
$$
Necessarily, ${\beta\choose 1}$ and $B_k {1/r_{2k+1}\choose 1}$ are collinear, and therefore 
$$
{\beta\choose1}=\pm \frac{\sqrt{1+\beta^2}}{\|B_k{1/r_{2k+1}\choose 1}\|} B_k{1/r_{2k+1}\choose 1}.
$$


By Lemma \ref{l.BT-compact}, there is a compact set $K\subset (-1,1)$ which depends only on $M$ so that $1/r_{2k+1}\in K$ for all $k$.

By Lemma \ref{l.disonance}, there are constants $C>0$ and $0<\eta<1$ which only depend on $M$ so that
$
\left\|B_k{1/r_{2k+1}\choose 1}\right\|\geq C^{-1}\eta^{-k}.
$
So
$
\left\|B_k^{-1}{\beta\choose 1}\right\|\leq C\eta^k \sqrt{1+\beta^2} \sqrt{1+r_{2k+1}^{-2}}\leq 2C\eta^k.
$
By \eqref{e.A-k-dagger},  $B_k^{-1}=A_k$, therefore  $\left\|A_k{\beta\choose 1}\right\|\leq C_1\eta^k,$ where $C_1$ depends only on $M$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
The {\em Even Gauss Map} $E:(-1,1)\to (-1,1)$, is given by \index{Even Gauss map}
\begin{equation}
\label{EvenGauss}
E(x):=\frac{1}{x}-2m\textrm{ on }\left[\frac{1}{2m+1},\frac{1}{2m-1}\right)\ \ (m\in\mathbb Z).
\end{equation}
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{l.position}
There exists a constant $0<{\varepsilon}(M)<1$ as follows.
Suppose $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are irrationals in $(-1,1)$ so that  $M(\beta), M(\gamma)\leq M$, then
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $
1+{\varepsilon}(M)<\left|\sigma\left[A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1}\right]\right|<1/{\varepsilon}(M)$,
\item ${\varepsilon}(M)<\left|\sigma\left[A_k(\beta){1\choose -\gamma}\right]\right|<1/(1+{\varepsilon}(M))$,
\item $
\left|\sin\measuredangle(A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1},A_k(\beta){1\choose -\gamma})\right|>{\varepsilon}(M).
$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Define ${\widehat\sigma}_k^s:={\widehat\sigma}\left[A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1}\right]$. By \eqref{e.A-k-dagger},
\begin{align}
&{\widehat\sigma}_k^s
     =(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_{2k}})^{-1}(\beta)=(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_{2k}})^{-1}(\lim_{n\to\infty} (v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_n})(0))\notag\\
     &=\lim_{n\to\infty} (v_{2m_{2k+1}}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_n})(0)=[0;2m_{2k+1},2m_{2k+2},\ldots]=E^{2k}(\beta)=:\beta_k'.\label{e.sigma-s} 
                              
\end{align}
In particular, $M({\widehat\sigma}^s_k), M(\frac{1}{{\widehat\sigma}^s_k}-2m_{2k+1})\leq M$.
By  Lemma \ref{l.BT-compact}, there exists a number  $0<\delta(M)<1$ which only depends on $M$ such that $\delta(M)<|{\widehat\sigma}_k^s|<1-\delta(M)$ for all $k$. Passing from the co-slope to the slope, we obtain the first part of the lemma. 

Suppose $\gamma=[0;2\ell_1,2\ell_2,\ldots]$ where $\ell_i\in \mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ and $M(\gamma)\leq M$. Set
${\widehat\sigma}^u_k:={\widehat\sigma}\left[A_k(\beta){1\choose -\gamma}\right]$. Let $u_{2m}(z):=\bigl({\tiny \begin{array}{cc}
     2m & 1\\ 1 & 0
     \end{array}}\bigr)\cdot z= 2m+\frac{1}{z}$.  By \eqref{e.A-k-prime},
\begin{align}
&{\widehat\sigma}^u_k
     =(u_{-2m_{2k}}\circ\cdots\circ u_{-2m_1})(-\gamma^{-1})
     =[-2m_{2k};-2m_{2k-1},\ldots,-2m_2,-2m_1,-\gamma^{-1}]\notag\\
     &=[-2m_{2k};-2m_{2k-1},\ldots,-2m_2,-2m_1,-2\ell_1,-2\ell_2,\ldots]\label{e.sigma-u}\\
     &=-[2m_{2k};2m_{2k-1},\ldots,2m_2,2m_1,2\ell_1,2\ell_2,\ldots].\notag
\end{align}
We see that $M({\widehat\sigma}_k^u+2m_{2k})\leq 2 M$ (the factor 2 is due to the possible increase in the length of the strings $(2,-2,\cdots,2,-2)$). Therefore there exists a constant $\delta'(M)$ which only depends on $M$ so that
$
{\widehat\sigma}^u_k\in -2m_{2k}+(-1+\delta',1-\delta').
$
Note that $|2m_{2k}|\leq M-1$, and therefore $|{\widehat\sigma}^u_k|\leq M$. Next, note that $|2m_{2k}|\geq 2$. If $2m_{2k}\leq -2$, then ${\widehat\sigma}^u_k\geq 1+\delta'$, and if $2m_{2k}\geq 2$, then ${\widehat\sigma}^u_k\leq -1-\delta'$. In all cases,
$
1+\delta'\leq |{\widehat\sigma}_k^u|\leq M.
$
Passing to the slope, we obtain the second part of the  lemma.



The third part of the lemma is an easy consequence of parts one and two.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{l.jordan-curve}
 The polygonal path $(\Pi_0,\Pi_1,\cdots,\Pi_5,\Pi_0)$ is a Jordan curve, therefore it bounds a  polygon $\Pi(E^u,E^s)$ with vertices $\Pi_i$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let  $S_i$ denote open line segment from $\Pi_i$ to $\Pi_{i+1}$. To prove the lemma, we need to show that $\overline{S}_i\cap\overline{S}_j$ are pairwise disjoint when $j\neq i\pm 1\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$, and that $\overline{S}_i\cap\overline{S}_j=\{\Pi_{j}\}$ when $j=i+1\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$. 

By construction, $\Pi_{i},\Pi_{i+1}$ both lie on $L_{i+1}$. Therefore $S_{i}\subset L_{i+1}$. 
If $i=j\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2$, then $\overline{S}_i, \overline{S}_{j}$ are disjoint because $L_{i}, L_{j}$ are disjoint parallel lines. 
If $j=i+1\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$ then  $\overline{S}_i\cap\overline{S}_{j}=\{\Pi_{j}\}$, because $L_{i}\cap L_{j}=\{\Pi_j\}$.
It remains to consider the case when  $j-i=3 \mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$. 


We  call the lines $L_{i}$ with slope  $\sigma^s$ ``almost vertical,'' and lines with slope $\sigma^u$ ``almost horizontal." The ``left,'' ``middle,'' and ``right'' almost vertical lines are 
$L_{4},L_{0},L_{2}$. The   ``top,'' ``middle,'' and ``bottom'' almost horizontal lines are   $(L_{3},L_{1},L_{5})$ when $\sigma^u<0$, and 
$
(L_{3},L_{5},L_{1})$ when  $\sigma^u_n>0$.


\medskip
\noindent
{\em Claim.\/} If  $j-i=3\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$, then  at least one of $\{L_{i+1},L_{j+1}\}$ is a not a middle line.

\medskip
\noindent
{\em Proof of the Claim\/}:  Since $j-i=3\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$,  $i,j$ have different parity. Therefore one of $L_{i+1},L_{j+1}$   is almost vertical, and the other is almost horizontal. Without loss of generality, $L_{i+1}$ is almost vertical, and $L_{j+1}$ is almost horizontal.   If $L_{i+1}=L_0$, then $i=5$,  $j=2$, and $L_{j+1}=L_3$ a top horizontal line. If $L_{i+1}\neq L_0$, then $L_{i+1}$ is a left or right almost vertical line. The claim follows.



\medskip
\noindent
Suppose now that $j-i=3\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6$, and assume by contradiction that $\overline{S}_i\cap\overline{S}_j\neq \varnothing$. By the claim,  one of $S_i, S_j$, say $\overline{S}_i$,  lies on a non-middle line $L$. A segment  on a non-middle line $L$ cannot intersect any other segment except at the boundary,  otherwise there would be vertices $\Pi_{i}$ on different sides of  $L$, and $L$ would have to be a middle line. So the  $\overline{S}_i$ intersects $\overline{S}_j$ at $\Pi_i$ or 
$\Pi_{i+1 \mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6}$. Necessarily, $\overline{S}_j$ intersects $\overline{S}_{i+1 \mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6}$ or $\overline{S}_{i-1\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 6}$. But  $j=(i\pm 1)\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2$, so as we saw above, this cannot happen.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Q}
$L_0$ cuts $\Pi$  into two parallelograms $\widetilde{Q}_1, \widetilde{Q}_2$, with sides parallel to $E^u, E^s$, such that $\widetilde{Q}_1$ contains $P_{0}$ in its boundary, and $\widetilde{Q}_2$  does not contain any $P_{i}$ with $i$ even in its boundary. \index{Associated fundamental domains!partition into parallelograms}
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
This follows easily from the fact that $|\sigma^s|>1$ and $|\sigma^u|<1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lem-7: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Fundamental-Domain}
$\Pi$ is a fundamental domain for the action of $G$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Thus, it  has side pairing (perhaps after further division of its sides) which turns it into a model of ${\mathsf{St}}_0$.
<!-- end lem-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Elementary geometric considerations show that  $T^k[\mathrm{int}(\Pi)]$ $(k\in\mathbb Z)$ are pairwise disjoint, and that 
$\displaystyle \Sigma:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}T^k[\Pi]$ is  a strip with two boundary  curves $\gamma,\gamma'$ made from a linear interpolation of the left (resp. right) $E^s$-sides of $\Pi$,  see Figure \ref{Figure-Tesselation}.

We claim that $\gamma'=S(\gamma)$. To see this, consider the polygon  $\widehat{\Pi}$ built as above, but with $P_i$ replaced by $S(P_i)$, and let  $\widehat{\Sigma}:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}T^k(\widehat{\Pi})$.
Since $P_1=S(P_5)$ and $P_2=S(P_4)$, the  right side $\gamma'$ of $\Sigma$ equals the left side of $\widehat{\Sigma}$. Since $\widehat{\Pi}=S(\Pi)$ and $T\circ S=S\circ T$,  $\widehat{\Sigma}=S(\Sigma)$, and the left side of $\widehat{\Sigma}$ equals $S(\gamma)$. It follows that $\gamma'=S(\gamma)$.

Since $\gamma'=S(\gamma)$, $S^\ell(\mathrm{int}(\Sigma))$ $(\ell\in\mathbb Z)$ are pairwise disjoint, and  
$\displaystyle \bigcup_{\ell\in\mathbb Z} S^\ell(\Sigma)=\mathbb R^2$. Thus $S^\ell T^k[\mathrm{int}(\Pi)]$ $(k,\ell\in\mathbb Z)$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\displaystyle \bigcup_{k,\ell\in\mathbb Z}S^\ell T^k(\Pi)=\mathbb R^2$. Since $T\circ S=S\circ T$,  $\{T^\ell S^k:k,\ell\in\mathbb Z\}=G$, and  $\Pi$ is a fundamental domain for $G$. 

The action of $G$ on $\partial\Pi$ determines a side pairing (perhaps after further subdivision) which makes $\Pi$ congruent to ${\mathsf{St}}_0$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lem-8: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)}\index{Bounded geometry}
There exists a constant $\Gamma(M)\!\!>\!\!1$ as follows. Suppose $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are irrationals in $(-1,1)$ so that $M(\beta),M(\gamma)\!\!\leq\!\! M$. Let
$\widetilde{E}^s_k:=\operatorname{span}\{A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1}\}$, and $\widetilde{E}^u_k:= \operatorname{span}\{A_k(\beta){1\choose -\gamma}\}$. Then for each $k\geq 0$,
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\widetilde{\Pi}:={\Pi}(\widetilde{E}^s_k,\widetilde{E}^u_k)$ is polygon bounded by a Jordan curve;
\item All the angles  of $\widetilde{\Pi}$ are at least $\Gamma(M)^{-1}$--away from $\pi\mathbb Z$;
\item $\Gamma(M)^{-1}\leq \|\widetilde{\Pi}_i-P_j\|\leq \Gamma(M)$ for all $0\leq i,j\leq 5$;
\item All the sides of $\widetilde{\Pi}$ have lengths in $[\Gamma(M)^{-1},\Gamma(M)]$;
\item $\widetilde{Q}_1,\widetilde{Q}_2$ contain open balls of radius $1/\Gamma(M)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-8 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $\sigma^s_k:=\sigma[A_k(\beta){\beta\choose 1}]$ and  
$\sigma^u_k:=\sigma[A_k(\beta){1\choose -\gamma}]$. 
 By Lemma \ref{l.position}, $|\sigma^s_k|>1$, and $|\sigma^u_k|<1$.
 Part (1) now follows
 from Lemma \ref{l.jordan-curve}. 

The angles of $\widetilde{\Pi}$ are uniformly bounded away from $\pi\mathbb Z$ by a constant which only depends on $M$, because of Lemma \ref{l.position}(3).
This is part (2). 


The quantities ${\rm dist}(\widetilde{\Pi}_i,P_j)$ and ${\rm dist} (\widetilde{\Pi}_i,\widetilde{\Pi}_{i+1})$ can be put in the form $g_{i,j}(\sigma^s_k,\sigma^u_k)$ and $h_i(\sigma^s_k,\sigma^u_k)$, where $g_{ij}, h_i$  are well-defined, positive,  and continuous functions  on
$$
X:=\{(\sigma^s,\sigma^u)\in\mathbb R^2: \sigma^u\neq\sigma^s, |\sigma^u|\cdot|\sigma^s|\neq 0\}.
$$
By  Lemma \ref{l.position}, $(\sigma^s_k,\sigma^u_k)$ belong to the compact set 
\begin{multline*}
 C:=\{(\sigma^s,\sigma^u)\in\mathbb R^2: |\sigma^s|\in [(1+\varepsilon(M))^{-1},\varepsilon(M)^{-1}], |\sigma^u|\in [\varepsilon(M),(1-\varepsilon(M))^{-1}]\}.
\end{multline*}
 On this set,  $g_{ij}$ and $h_i$ are bounded away from zero and infinity by constants which  depend only on $M$.  Parts (3) and (4) follow. 
 
 Part (5) follows from Parts (2) and (4).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lem-9: body_md -->
\label{LmDenseWs}
 For every $M>1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$ there exists $T$ as follows: If  $r\in{\mathsf{BT}}(M)$,  
   then every line in ${\mathsf{St}}_0$ with slope $r$ and length $T$  is $\varepsilon$-dense in ${\mathsf{St}}_0$.
<!-- end lem-9 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{Prop-Contracting-Automorphisms}
There exists $\varepsilon(\alpha), K(\alpha)>0$ and maps  $\widetilde{\psi}_n:\mathrm{St}\to \mathrm{St}$ as follows:

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item \textbf{\textit{Automorphisms:}} $\widetilde{\psi}_n$ are homogeneous affine staircase automorphisms with derivatives $A_n\in\Gamma(2)$. They  fix the singularities of the staircase, and have zero drift.
\item \textbf{\textit{Uniform Hyperbolicity:}} For every $n\geq 0$, $\mathbb R^2=E^u_n\oplus E^s_n$ where\index{Uniform hyperbolicity}
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item $E^s_0=\operatorname{span}\{{\beta\choose 1}\}$, $E^u_0=\operatorname{span}\{{1\choose -\beta}\}$, and $A_n(E^t_n)=E^t_{n+1}$ $(t=u,s)$;
    \item $\|A_n|_{E^s_n}\|\leq \lambda^{-1}$ and  $\|A_n|_{E^u_{n}}\|\geq \lambda$;
    \item $|\sin\measuredangle(E^s_n,E^u_n)|>\varepsilon(\alpha)$.
    \end{enumerate}
\item \textbf{\textit{Slopes:}} If $\sigma^s_n:=\sigma[A_n\cdots A_1 A_0 {\beta \choose 1}]$ and $\sigma^u_n:=\sigma[A_n\cdots  A_1 A_0{1\choose -\beta}]$, then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $|\sigma^s_n|>1$ and $|\sigma^u_n|<1$;
\item   $\varepsilon(\alpha)<|\sigma^t_n|, |\sigma_n^t-1|<\varepsilon(\alpha)^{-1}$ $(t=s,u)$; 
\item   The digits in the regular and even CFE of $\sigma_{n}^{t}$, $t=u,s$, $n\geq 0$ have absolute values less than $K(\alpha)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item \textbf{\textit{Finitely Many Types:}} $\#\{\widetilde{\psi}_n:n=0,1,2,\ldots\}<\infty$;
\item \textbf{\textit{Bounded Geometry:}} The polygons $\Pi(n):=\Pi(E^s_n,E^u_n)$ constructed in Section \ref{ss.Pi(n)} satisfy all the bounded geometry estimates in Lemma \ref{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)}.\index{Bounded geometry}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let ${\varepsilon}(\alpha):={\varepsilon}(M)$ from Lemma~\ref{l.position}.
Since  $\alpha\in (0,1)$, $\beta\in (-1,1)$. 
Let $\beta:=[0;2m_1,2m_2,2m_3,\ldots]$ be the even CFE of $\beta$. 
By Lemma \ref{l.A-contracts}, there exist $C>1$ and $0<\eta<1$ which only depend on $M$, so that 
$$
\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){\beta'\choose 1}\right\|\leq C\eta^{N_0}\left\|{\beta'\choose 1}\right\| \textrm{for every  $N_0$ and  every $\beta'$ such that $M(\beta')\leq M$}.
$$

We claim that  there is a constant $C'>0$ which only depends on $M$ so that  for every $|\beta''|\leq M$ such that $|\sin\measuredangle ({\beta'\choose 1},{1\choose -\beta''})|>{\varepsilon}(M)$,
$$
\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){ 1\choose -\beta''}\right\|\geq C'\eta^{-N_0}\left\|{ 1\choose -\beta''}\right\|.
$$
To see this note that the area of the parallelogram generated by the vectors
$A_{N_0}(\beta'){ \beta'\choose 1}$ and   $A_{N_0}(\beta'){ 1\choose -\beta''}$ is the same as the area of the parallelogram generated by ${ \beta'\choose 1}$ and   ${1\choose -\beta''}$, whence bounded below by $|\sin{\varepsilon}(M)|$. Since $\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){ \beta'\choose 1}\right\|$ is exponentially small, $\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){1\choose -\beta''}\right\|$ is  exponentially large, with bounds depending only on $M$.

We now choose $N_0$ large enough so that $C\eta^{N_0}<\lambda^{-1}$ and $C'\eta^{-N_0}>\lambda$. Then for every $\beta',\beta''$ such that $M(\beta')\leq M$, $|\beta''|\leq M$ and 
$
|\sin({\beta'\choose 1},{1\choose -\beta''})|\geq {\varepsilon}(M)$,
\begin{equation}\label{e.N_0-choice}
\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){\beta'\choose 1}\right\|< \lambda^{-1}\left\|{\beta'\choose 1}\right\|,\textrm{ and }
\left\|A_{N_0}(\beta'){1\choose -\beta''}\right\|> \lambda\left\|{1\choose -\beta''}\right\|.
\end{equation}
Define ${A}_0\!\!:=\!\!A_{N_0}(\beta)$, $\beta_0',\beta_0''\!\!:=\!\!\beta$,  $E^s_0\!\!:=\!\!\operatorname{span}\{{\beta_0'\choose 1}\}$ and 
$E^u_0\!\!:=\!\!\operatorname{span}\{{1\choose -\beta_0''}\}$. Clearly, $M(\beta_0'), M(\beta_0'')\leq M$ and $E^u_0\perp E^s_0$, and therefore by \eqref{e.N_0-choice},
$$
\|A_0|_{E^s_0}\|<\lambda^{-1}\textrm{ and }\|A_0|_{E^u_0}\|>\lambda.
$$


Let 
$E^s_1:=A_0(E^s_0)$ and $E^u_1:=A_0(E^u_0)$. 
By Lemma \ref{l.position} and since $M(\beta_0'), M(\beta_0'')\leq M$, 
\begin{equation}\label{e.zero-ineq}
|\sin\measuredangle(E^s_1,E^u_1)|>{\varepsilon}(M).
\end{equation}
Write  $
E^s_1=\operatorname{span}\{{\beta_1'\choose 1}\}$ and $E^u_1=\operatorname{span}\{{1\choose -\beta_1''}\}
$, with 
$
\beta_1':={\widehat\sigma}\left[A_0{\beta_0'\choose 1}\right]$, and  $-(\beta_1'')^{-1}:={\widehat\sigma}\left[A_0{1\choose -\beta_0'}\right]
$.
Co-slope calculations  as  in  \eqref{e.sigma-s} and \eqref{e.sigma-u} show that
\begin{align*}
&\beta_1'={\widehat\sigma}\bigl[\bigl(\!{\tiny{\!\begin{array}{c}\beta_1'\\ 1\end{array}}}\!\!\bigr)\bigr]={\widehat\sigma} \bigl[A_0\bigl(\!{\tiny{\!\begin{array}{c}\beta_0'\\ 1\end{array}}}\!\!\bigr)\bigr]=A_0\!\cdot\! \beta_0'=E^{2N_0}(\beta_0')=E^{2N_0}(\beta)=[0;2m_{2N_0+1},2m_{2N_0+2},\ldots]\\
&\beta_1'' =-\frac{1}{{\widehat\sigma}{\tiny{1\choose -\beta_1''} }}=-\frac{1}{{\widehat\sigma} [A_0{\tiny{1\choose -\beta} }]} =[0;2m_{2N_0},2m_{2N_0-1},\ldots,2m_2, 2m_1, 2m_1,2m_2,2m_3,\ldots ].
\end{align*}
It follows that  $\beta_1', \beta_1''$ are irrationals in $(-1,1)$ such that $M(\beta_1'), M(\beta_1'')\leq M$. 
Let $A_1:=A_{N_0}(\beta_1')=A_{N_0}(E^{2N_0}(\beta))$. By \eqref{e.N_0-choice} and \eqref{e.zero-ineq},
$$
\|A_1|_{E^s_1}\|<\lambda^{-1}\textrm{ and }\|A_1|_{E^u_1}\|>\lambda.
$$


We now let $E^s_2\!\!:=\!\!A_1(E^s_1)$, $E^u_2\!\!:=\!\!A_1(E^u_1)$. By Lemma \ref{l.position} and since $M(\beta_1'),M(\beta_1'')\!\!\leq\!\! M$, 
$|\sin\measuredangle(E^s_2,E^u_2)|>{\varepsilon}(M)$. Equations \eqref{e.sigma-s} and \eqref{e.sigma-u} lead as before to
$
E^s_2:=\operatorname{span}\{{\beta_2'\choose 1}\}$ and $E^u_2:=\operatorname{span}\{{1\choose -\beta''_2}\}
$, with 
\begin{align*}
&\beta_2'=A_1\cdot \beta_1'=E^{2N_0}(\beta_1')=E^{4N_0}(\beta)=[0;2m_{4N_0+1},2m_{4N_0+2},\ldots]\\
&\beta_2''=-\frac{1}{{\widehat\sigma}(A_1{\tiny{1\choose -\beta''_1})}} =[0;2m_{4N_0},2m_{4N_0-1},\ldots,2m_2, 2m_1, 2m_1,2m_2,2m_3,\ldots ].
\end{align*}
Again $\beta_2',\beta_2''$ are irrationals in $(-1,1)$ such that $M(\beta_2'),M(\beta_2'')\leq 
M$.  Let $$A_2:=A_{N_0}(\beta_2')=A_{N_0}(E^{4N_0}(\beta)).$$
Then as before,
$\|A_2|_{E^s_2}\|<\lambda^{-1}\textrm{ and }\|A_2|_{E^u_2}\|>\lambda$, 


Continuing in this way,  we obtain Part (2) of the proposition with the matrices
$\displaystyle A_k:=A_{N_0}(E^{2kN_0}(\beta))$, and the spaces  $E^s_k=\operatorname{span}\{{\beta_k'\choose 1}\}$, $E^u_k=\operatorname{span}\{{1\choose -\beta_k''}\}$, where 
\begin{align*}
&\beta_k'=[0;2m_{2kN_0+1},2m_{2kN_0+2},\ldots]; \\ 
&\beta_k'' =[0;2m_{2kN_0},2m_{2kN_0-1},\ldots,2m_2, 2m_1, 2m_1,2m_2,2m_3,\ldots ].
\end{align*}
The slopes (not co-slopes) of 
$E^s_k,E^u_k$ are 
\begin{equation}\label{e.E-k} 
\begin{aligned}
& \sigma^s_k\!=\!\frac{1}{\beta_k'}\!=\![2m_{2kN_0+1};2m_{2kN_0+2},\ldots]\\
& \sigma^u_k\!=\!-\beta_k''\!=\! [0;-2m_{2kN_0},-2m_{2kN_0-1},\ldots,\!-2m_2, -2m_1, -2m_1,-2m_2,-2m_3,\ldots ].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Clearly,  $|\sigma^s_k|>1$, $|\sigma^u_k|<1$, and 
$M(\sigma^u_k),M(\sigma^s_k)\leq M$ (see \eqref{e.M-beta}). By Lemma \ref{l.BT-bounded-pm-two}, the partial  quotients of the regular CFE of $\sigma^s_k,\sigma^u_k$ are bounded by 
$M+3$. Necessarily, the distance of 
 $\sigma^s_k, \sigma^u_k$ from  $-1, 0, 1$ is bounded below by a constant which only depends on $M$, whence only on $\alpha$.  This proves  Part (3). 

Let $\widetilde{\psi}_n$ denote the unique homogeneous automorphism of the staircase with zero drift and derivative matrix $A_n$, see Proposition \ref{Prop-Automorphisms}. This automorphism fixes the singularities of ${\mathsf{St}}$. 
By construction, $A_n=A_{N_0}([0;2m_{2nN_0+1},2m_{2nN_0+2},2m_{2nN_0+3},\ldots])$. Looking at \eqref{e.A-k} and recalling that $|2m_i|\leq M$ for all $i$, we see that $\{A_0,A_1,\ldots\}$ is finite. Therefore $\{\widetilde{\psi}_0,\widetilde{\psi}_1,\ldots\}$ is finite.


We proved parts (1)--(4). Part (5) follows from Lemma \ref{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)}, with $\gamma=\beta$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{r.mat-prod-form} \normalfont 
The proof gives  $A_j=A_{N_0}(E^{2jN_0}(\beta))=A_{N_0}([0;2m_{2jN_0+1},2m_{2jN_0+2},\ldots])$. 
By \eqref{e.A-k-prime}, 
$
A_j=\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
-2m_{2(j+1)N_0} & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}
\right)\cdots
\left(
\begin{array}{cc}
-2m_{2jN_0+2} & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}
\right)
 \left(
\begin{array}{cc}
-2m_{2jN_0+1} & 1 \\
1 & 0
\end{array}
\right).
$
Taking the product over $j$ and using \eqref{e.A-k-prime} one more time, we obtain the identities
\begin{equation}\label{e.mat-prod-form}
\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0=\widetilde{\Psi}_{nN_0}\ ; \ A_{n-1}\cdots A_2 A_0=	A_{nN_0}(\beta), 
\textrm{  see \eqref{e.A-k}}.
\end{equation}
Notice that by construction,  we can take the same $N_0$ for all $\beta$ such that $M(\beta)\leq M$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lem-10: body_md -->
\label{l.strict-convexity-P}
For all $n$ large enough, $\mathcal P_n(\xi)$ given in \eqref{TempPres} is strictly convex. \index{Geometric pressure!strict convexity}
<!-- end lem-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Recall that $\mathcal P_n(\xi)=\log\left(\int_{{\mathsf{R}}_0}e^{\xi z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})}d\mu_0\right)$, with  $z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$ as in \eqref{e.z-n}. A direct calculation shows that 
$\displaystyle
\mathcal P''(\xi)=\frac{\int_{{\mathsf{R}}_0} e^{\xi z_n}z_n^2 d\mu_0}{\int_{{\mathsf{R}}_0}e^{\xi z_n}d\mu_0}-\left(\frac{\int_{{\mathsf{R}}_0}e^{\xi z_n}z_nd\mu_0}{\int_{{\mathsf{R}}_0}e^{\xi z_n}d\mu_0}\right)^2.
$
The expression on the right is the variance of the random variable $z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$, when ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is sampled randomly uniformly from the probability measure on ${\mathsf{R}}_0$ with density proportional to $e^{\xi z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})}$. 

Every non-constant random variable has strictly positive variance. Therefore,  to show that $\mathcal P''(\xi)>0$, it is sufficient to show that for all $n$ large enough,  $z_n$ is not equal a.e. to a constant on ${\mathsf{R}}_0$.

Recall that $z_n({\widetilde{\omega}})={\mathfrak{z}}(\widetilde{\Psi}_n({\widetilde{\omega}}))$ a.e. on ${\mathsf{R}}_0$. 
{ Fix some linear segment $W\subset{\mathsf{R}}_0$} such that $W$ is parallel to $E^u_0$. Then $|\widetilde{\Psi}_n(W)|\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\infty$, so for all $n$ sufficiently large, 
${\mathfrak{z}}$ is not constant on $\widetilde{\Psi}_n(W)$. Replacing $W$ by an $(E^u_0,E^s_0)$-parallelogram with $E^u_0$-side $W$, we see that ${\mathfrak{z}}$ is not almost surely constant on $\widetilde{\Psi}_n({{\mathsf{R}}_0})$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- thm-28: body_md -->
\label{ThDriftOfOrigin}
Let $\beta\in (-1,1)$ be an irrational with even CFE  $\beta:=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$, and let $L_0$ denote the ray in direction $\beta\choose 1$,  which begins at 
the singularity ${\widetilde{\omega}}_0$, in the middle of the top side of rectangle $\mathsf R_0$. Let $\frak{z}_n$ denote the $\mathbb Z$-coordinate of the horizontal rectangle which contains the beginning of  
$(\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0)(L_0)$. Then
$$
\frak{z}_n=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{nN_0} \bigl[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k-1})\bigr].
$$
<!-- end thm-28 -->
<!-- cor-8: body_md -->
If the frequency of odd $j$ with a sign change $\operatorname{sgn}(m_{j})\neq \operatorname{sgn}(m_{j+1})$  is zero, then $\frak{z}_n/n\to 0$.
<!-- end cor-8 -->
<!-- cor-9: body_md -->
\label{CrSqrt23}

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
$|\frak{z}_n|\leq nN_0$;
\item If $\beta=2\sqrt{3}-3$ (the direction corresponding to $\alpha=\sqrt{3}\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 1$), then $\frak{z}_n=0$;
\item  If $\beta=2\sqrt{2}-3$ (the direction corresponding to $\alpha=\sqrt{2}\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 1$), then $\frak{z}_n=
nN_0$;
\item  
If $\beta=3-2\sqrt{2}$ (the direction corresponding to $\alpha=-\sqrt{2}\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 1$), then $\frak{z}_n=
-nN_0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end cor-9 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Part (1) is clear. Parts (2)--(4)  follow from the identities
\begin{equation}
\label{Sqrt23ECF}
2\sqrt{3}-3=[0;2,6,2,6,\ldots],\quad
2\sqrt{2}-3=[0;-6,6,-6,6,\ldots], 
\end{equation}
and $-(2\sqrt{2}-3)=[0;6,-6,6,-6,\ldots]$.  (We guessed \eqref{Sqrt23ECF} using the even Gauss map as in the proof of Lemma \ref{l.f-expansion}. The guesses can be confirmed by  solving $t=[0;-6,6,t]$ or $t=[0;2,6,t]$ subject to the constraint $t\in (-1,1)$.)
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\normalfont
If $\alpha$ is a quadratic irrational,\index{Quadratic irrationals!renormalization by a single map} then the sequence of matrices in \eqref{e.A-k} is eventually periodic. One can then choose all the  ${\psi}_n$ to be  equal \cite{Avila-Dolgopyat-Duryev-Sarig}, and take all the partitions $\mathfrak P_n$ to be equal to the Adler \& Weiss Markov partition from   \cite{Adler-Weiss-MP}.  
But in the general bounded type case, the sequence $\{\psi_n\}$  cannot be chosen to be  constant, and we  use a modification of  the symbolic coding due to  Arnoux \& Fisher \cite{Arnoux-Fisher}. The difference between our coding and the Arnoux-Fisher coding is in the choice of the fundamental domain for $\mathbb R^2/\sqrt{2}\mathbb Z^2$. We use the fundamental domains in  Section \ref{ss.Pi(n)}. This leads to a simpler symbolic description of the jump functions $f_k$.\index{Markov partition!Adler-Weiss and Arnoux-Fisher constructions}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\normalfont
Sinai and Bowen  provided symbolic coding for a single {\em non-linear} uniformly hyperbolic diffeomorphism in any dimension \cite{Sinai-MP1, Sinai-MP2, Bowen-MP}, which codes the measure of maximal entropy by a Markov chain. This was generalized to sequences of different uniformly hyperbolic diffeomorphisms in 
\cite{GK97, MuentesRibeiro}. 
But  the mixing properties of the 
symbolic systems obtained this way require further analysis to allow the extension of our methods to this context; therefore  we could not use the symbolic codings in these
 references.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lem-11: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Bottom-Side}
Exactly one stable side of $Q_i(n)$ has the following property: If we move from {\em any} point in the relative interior of this side in the positive unstable direction, then we will initially enter the interior of $Q_i(n)$.
<!-- end lem-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
It is clear that such a side exists, the only thing to check is that it is unique.
Otherwise, $\overline{Q_i(n)}$ projects to  a non-trivial closed invariant set for the linear flow in the positive unstable direction. But this flow has dense orbits in ${\mathsf{St}}_0$, because of the irrationality of the  positive unstable direction.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lem-12: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Choice-of-lambda}
For all $0\leq i\leq 5$ and $n\geq 0$,
\begin{align}
&\Gamma(M)^{-2}<{\max\{\|\Pi_i(n)-P_j\|:0\leq i,j\leq 5\}\over
\min\{\|\Pi_i(n+1)-P_j\|:0\leq i,j\leq 5\}}<\Gamma(M)^2 
\label{Eq-Choice-of-lambda}\\
&\begin{array}{l}
\textrm{Every line in $\mathsf{St}_0$ in direction $E^u_n$ with length $T_0(M)$}\\
\textrm{must enter $Q_1(n)$ and $Q_2(n)$}.
\end{array}
\label{Eq-Choice-of-lambda-also}
\end{align}
<!-- end lem-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Proposition \ref{Prop-Contracting-Automorphisms} guarantees that $\Pi(n)$ satisfies all the bounded geometry estimates in Lemma \ref{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)}. In particular, 
$\Gamma(M)^{-1}\!<\!\|\Pi_i(n)\!-\!P_j\|\!<\!\Gamma(M)$ for all $i,j,n$, whence   \eqref{Eq-Choice-of-lambda}. Next,  $Q_i(n)$ contain open balls of radius $1/\Gamma(M)$, so (\ref{Eq-Choice-of-lambda-also}) follows from Lemma \ref{LmDenseWs} and the choice of $T_0(M)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lem-13: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Invariant-Stable-Sides}
The bottom (resp. top) stable side of $Q_i(n)$ is mapped by $\psi_n$ to the 
relative interior of the  bottom (resp. top) stable side of $Q_1(n+1)$.
<!-- end lem-13 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Recall that $\psi_n$ fixes the punctures of ${\mathsf{St}}_0$:
 $\psi_n(p_0)=p_0$ and $\psi_n(p_1)=p_1$ where $p_0$ is the  congruence  class of $P_0=(1,0)$,   and $p_1$ is the congruence class of  $P_1=(2,0)$.


Let $L_0(n)$ denote the line through $p_0$ in direction $E^s_n$. Given $r$, let $B^s_n(p_0,r)$ denote the symmetric linear segment in $L_0(n)$ with center $p_0$ and radius 
$$
r:=\max\{\|\Pi_i(n)-P_j\|:0\leq i,j\leq 5\}.
$$
By construction, the stable sides of $Q_i(n)$ are contained in $B^s_n(p_0,r)$, see Figure \ref{Figure-Pi(n)}.

Since $\psi_n(p_0)=p_0$, $d\psi_n=A_n$, $A_n(E^s_n)=E^s_{n+1}$, and $\|A_n|_{E^s_n}\|\leq \lambda^{-1}$,  $\psi_n(B^s_n(p_0,r))\subset B^s_{n+1}(p_0,\lambda^{-1}r)$. 
By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Choice-of-lambda} and the choice of $\lambda$ in \eqref{e.choice-of-lambda}, 
$$
\lambda^{-1} r<\frac{1}{\Gamma(M)^2}\max\{\|\Pi_i(n)-P_j\|:0\leq i,j\leq 5\}\leq \min\{\|\Pi_i(n+1)-P_j\|:0\leq i,j\leq 5\}. 
$$
Calling the right-hand-side $r'$, we deduce that 
$\psi_n(B^s_n(p_0,r))\subset B^s_n(p_0,r')$. 

We now observe that $B^s_n(p_0,r')$ is a subset of 
 the  top {\em and} of the bottom stable sides of $Q_1(n+1)$, because each of these segments contains one of $P_0,P_2,P_4$, which all project to $p_0$, and because the distance of these points to the edge is no less than $r'$. 
 
It follows that $\psi_n$ maps the top and bottom stable sides of $Q_i(n)$ into the intersection of the top and bottom sides of $Q_1(n+1)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lem-14: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Partition}
For every $n$,
$\psi_n(Q_i(n))=Q_{i,1}^{n+1}\cup\cdots\cup Q_{i, N_i(n+1)}^{n+1}$, where:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ are  $(E^u_{n+1},E^s_{n+1})$-parallelograms.
\item The stable sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ are subsets of stable sides of $Q_1(n+1)$ or $Q_2(n+1)$.
\item For  $j<N_i(n+1)$, the top stable side of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ is the bottom stable side of $Q_{i,{j+1}}^{n+1}$.
\item The interiors of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ are pairwise disjoint.
\item $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ is a subset of $Q_1(n+1)$ or of $Q_2(n+1)$.
\item For each $\omega \in Q_i(n)$ there are $\varpi_j\in Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ s.t. 
$\displaystyle\psi_n(W^u(\omega,Q_i(n)))\!=\!\!\!\!\!\bigcup_{j=1}^{N_i(n+1)}\!\!\!\!\! W^u(\varpi_j,Q_{i,j}^{n+1}).$
\item If $Q_{i,j}^n\subset Q_k(n)$, then $\mathrm{int}(Q_{i,j}^n)\cap\psi_n^{-1}(\mathrm{int}(Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1}))\neq\varnothing$ for  $\ell=1,\ldots, N_k(n+1)$.
\item The bottom stable side of $Q_{1,1}^{n+1}$ and the top side of $Q_{1, N_1}^{n+1}$ contain $p_0$. All other stable sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ do not.
\item   $N_1(n)$ and $N_2(n)$ are bounded by a constant which only depends only on $M$.
\item The lengths of the stable and unstable sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$  are uniformly bounded away from zero and infinity by  constants only depend on $M$, but not on $i,j$ and $n$.
\item Each $Q_{i,j}^{n}$ contains a ball of  radius $w>0$, which depends on $M$ but not on $i,j,n$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-14 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Fix two  $u$-fibres $W,W'$ in $Q_i(n)$.
By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Invariant-Stable-Sides}, $\psi_n$ maps $u$-fibres in $F_n$ to the union of $u$-fibres in $F_{n+1}$. Write   
$$
\psi_n(W)=W_1\cup\cdots\cup W_N\ , \quad \psi_n(W')=W_1'\cup\cdots\cup W_{N'}',
$$
where
  $W_i$ and $W_i'$  are  $u$-fibers in $F_n$;   $W_1,\ldots, W_N$ (respectively $W_1',\ldots, W_{N'}'$) are ordered in the positive unstable direction in $ F_{n+1}$; and $\overline{W_1},\ldots, \overline{W_N}$ (respectively $\overline{W_1'},\ldots, \overline{W_{N'}'}$) meet only at their endpoints, if at all. For each $j$, there are $a_j,a_j'\in\{1,2\}$ such that $W_j\subset \overline{Q_{a_j}(n+1)}$ and $W_j'\subset \overline{Q_{a_j'}(n+1)}$. 
We claim that $N=N'$ and $a_j=a_j'$.


By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Invariant-Stable-Sides},  $W_1,W_1'$  begin at $Q_1(n+1)$,  and $W_N,W_{N'}$  end at $Q_1(n+1)$. Therefore $a_1=a_1'$ and $a_N=a_{N'}$. If $a_j=a_j'$ for all $1\leq j\leq \min\{N,N'\}$, then $|W_j|=|W_j'|$ for all $1\leq j\leq \min\{N,N'\}$. Since $|\psi_n(W)|=|\psi_n(W')|$, it must be the case that  $N'=N$ and we are done. 
Assume by contradiction that  there is a (minimal) $1<j<\min\{N,N'\}$ such that  $a_j\neq a_j'$. Then $W,W'$ are separated by a $u$-fiber $V$ such that 
$$
\psi_n(V)=V_1\cup\cdots\cup V_{N''},
$$
where $V_i$ is a $u$-fiber in $Q_{a_i}(n+1)$ between $W_i,W_i'$ for $i=1,\ldots,j-1$, and $V_j$  passes through the unstable boundary of $Q_1(n)$ or $Q_2(n)$. Again, since $\psi_n(V)$ begins and ends inside the open stable sides of $Q_1(n+1)$, $1<j<N''$. 
Looking at Figure \ref{Figure-Pi(n)}  in Section \ref{ss.Pi(n)}
, we see that $V_{j-1}\cup V_j\cup V_{j+1}$ must contain $p_1$ (the projection of $P_1,P_3,P_5$) in its interior.  It follows that  $\psi_n(V)\owns p_1$. But then $p_1\in\mathrm{int}(\psi_n(Q_i(n)))$, whence $p_1\in \mathrm{int}(Q_i(n))$  which is not true. So $a_j=a_j'$ for all $1\leq j\leq \min\{N,N'\}$, whence
$N=N'$ and the claim is proved.


We can now define $N_i(n+1):=N$ and take $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ to be the union of $W_j$ where $W$ ranges over all $u$-fibres in $Q_i(n)$.
Since $\psi_n$ is piecewise affine, $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ are solid parallelograms, and it is clear from the construction that they satisfy (1)--(7).



For (8), recall that $p_0$ is a fixed point of $\psi_n$ inside the top and bottom stable sides of $Q_1(n)$, and outside the stable sides of $Q_2(n)$. Since
the bottom side of $Q_{1,1}^{n+1}$ and the top side of $Q_{1, N_1}^{n+1}$ are equal to the $\psi_n$--image of the bottom and top stable sides of $Q_1(n)$, they must contain $p_0$.
The same argument shows that the bottom side of $Q_{2,1}^{n+1}$ and the top side of $Q_{2,N_2}^{n+1}$ do {\em not} contain $p_0$.
All other stable sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$  cannot contain $p_0$,  because they are mapped by $\psi_n^{-1}$ to the interior of $Q_i(n)$, which does not contain $p_0$.

To see part (9), we  recall that  the lengths of the $u$-sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$ are bounded away from zero and infinity by a constant which depends only on $M$ (Lemma \ref{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)}). By construction, the norms of $d\psi_n$ are uniformly bounded (because there are only finitely many such matrices). Now apply the sixth part of the lemma. 

To see part (10), we use the proof of part (9) to bound the $u$-sides, and  note that the $s$-sides of $Q_{i,j}^{n+1}$  are  bounded below, because are  equal to the image of one of the sides of  $\Pi(n)$ by $\psi_n$, and $\{\psi_k:k\geq 0\}$ is a finite set.

Part 11  follows from the uniform bounds on $\measuredangle(E^u_n,E^s_n)$ 
{in Lemma \ref{l.position}.}
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{Prop-Markov}
Let $\mathfrak P_0:=\{Q_1(0), Q_2(0)\}$ and
$$\mathfrak P_{n}:=\{Q_{1,1}^{n},\ldots,Q_{1,N_1(n)}^{n};Q_{2,1}^{n},\ldots,Q_{2,N_2(n)}^{n}\}\ \ (n\geq 0),$$ then the following properties hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item \textit{\textbf{Partition:}} $\{\overline{P}: P\in\mathfrak P_n\}$ covers ${\mathsf{St}}_0$, and $\{\mathrm{int}(P):P\in\mathfrak P_n\}$ are pairwise disjoint.
\item \textit{\textbf{Product Structure:}} For every $P\in\mathfrak P_{n}$ and $\omega, \varpi \in P$, $W^u(\omega,P)\cap W^s(\varpi,P)$ consists of a single point, which also belongs to $P$.\index{Markov partition}\index{Product structure}
\item \textit{\textbf{Markov Property:}} If $P\in\mathfrak P_n$, $Q\in\mathfrak P_{n+1}$,  \index{Markov property!for a Markov partition}
$\omega \in \mathrm{int}(P)$,  and $\psi_n(\omega)\in \mathrm{int}(Q)$, then
 $\psi_n^{-1}(W^u(\psi_n(\omega),Q))\subset W^u(\omega,P)$, 
 $\psi_n(W^s(\omega ,P))\subset W^s(\psi_n(\omega),Q)$.
\item \textit{\textbf{Bounded Cardinality:}}  $|\mathfrak P_n|\leq C$, where $C$ depends only on $M(\beta)$ in \eqref{e.M-beta}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Part (1) follows from {Lemma \ref{Lemma-Fundamental-Domain}}
                
 and the fact that $\psi_n$ is a homeomorphism. Part (2) is because the elements of $\mathfrak P_n$ are parallelograms with sides parallel to $E^s_n, E^u_n$. Part~(4) is a direct consequence of Lemma \ref{Lemma-Partition}(9). Part (3) can be proved as follows.

 Write $P=Q_{i,j}^n$ and $Q=Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1}$.
By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Partition}(5), $Q_{i,j}^n\subset Q_m(n)$ for $m=1$ or $2$.
Necessarily, if ${\widetilde{\omega}}\in\mathrm{int}(P)$ and $\psi_n({\widetilde{\omega}})\in\mathrm{int}(Q)$, then 
$$\psi_n(\omega)\in \psi_n(\mathrm{int}(Q_m(n)))\cap\mathrm{int}(Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})\subset \psi_n(\mathrm{int}(Q_m(n)))\cap\psi_n(\mathrm{int}(Q_k(n))).$$ 
So  $\omega\in\mathrm{int}(Q_m(n))\cap \mathrm{int}(Q_k(n))$. It follows that $m=k$ (otherwise the intersection is empty). So $Q_{i,j}^n\subset Q_k(n)$.

By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Partition}(6),  
$\displaystyle \psi_n(W^u(\omega, Q_{i,j}^n))
=\bigcup_{\ell'=1}^{N_k}
W^u(\varpi_{\ell'},Q_{k,\ell'}^{n+1})$ 
for some 
$\varpi_{\ell'} \in Q_{k,\ell'}^{n+1}$. Since $\psi_n(\omega)\in \mathrm{int}(Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$ and the interiors of $Q_{k,\ell'}^{n+1}$ are disjoint, it must be the case that $\psi_n(\omega)\in W^u({\varpi_\ell},Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$. It follows that  
$W^u(\varpi_{\ell},Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})=W^u(\psi_n(\omega),Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$. So
$$\psi_n(W^u(\omega,Q_{i,j}^n))\supset W^u(\psi_n(\omega),Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1}).$$ 
This is the first inclusion in (3).

For the second inclusion,
we  use $Q_{i,j}^n\!\!\subset\!\! Q_k(n)$ again to see that  
$\psi_n(W^s(\omega ,Q_{i,j}^n))\!\!\subset\!\! \psi_n(W^s(\omega,Q_k(n)))$. This is a line segment through 
$\psi_n(\omega)$, in direction  $E^s_{n+1}$, and with endpoints on the unstable boundary of 
$\displaystyle \psi_n(Q_k(n))\!\!=\!\!\bigcup_{{\ell=1}}^{N_k} Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1}$. Since $\psi_n(\omega)\in\mathrm{int}(Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$, the  only such line segment is  $W^s(\psi_n(\omega),Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$. 
Therefore $\psi_n(W^s(\omega,Q_{i,j}^n))\subset W^s(\psi_n(\omega),Q_{k,\ell}^{n+1})$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lem-15: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Modified-Approx-Canonical}
$\sup\limits_n\sup\limits_{\omega\in{\mathsf{St}}^\ast}|\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_n(\omega)-{\mathfrak{z}}(\omega)|<\infty$.
<!-- end lem-15 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{Lemma-Bounded-Geometry-Gamma(M)},  for some $N$,  
for every $n$, $\displaystyle \widetilde{F}_n\subset \bigcup_{|n|\leq N}D^n({\mathsf{R}}_0)$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
\index{Jump functions}\index{Jump functions!symbolic}\index{Frobenius function!jump functions}
Suppose $\omega\in{\mathsf{St}}_0^\ast$, and choose some (any)  $\widetilde{\omega}\in{\mathsf{St}}^\ast$ which projects to $\omega\in{\mathsf{St}}_0^\ast$. 
Let ${\widetilde{\omega}}_n:={\widetilde{\omega}}$ and ${\widetilde{\omega}}_k:=(\widetilde{\psi}_k^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}^{-1})(\widetilde{\omega})$. Set
\begin{equation}\label{Eq-Modified-Frobenius}
\widetilde{f}^{(n)}_0\equiv 0,\ \ 
\widetilde{f}_{k}^{(n)}(\omega):=
\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k}({\widetilde{\omega}}_{k})-\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k-1}({\widetilde{\omega}}_{k-1})\ (1\leq k\leq n) .
\end{equation}
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- lem-16: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-f(X)}
There are functions $f_{k}:\mathfrak P_{k}\to\mathbb Z$  such that $f_0\equiv 0$ and  for all $n\geq k$,
$\widetilde{f}_{k}^{(n)}(\omega)=f_{k}(X^{(n)}_{k}(\omega))\textrm{ a.e. in ${\mathsf{St}}_0^\ast$, where $X^{(n)}_{k}$ are given in \eqref{e.X-new}}.
$ 
These functions are uniformly bounded by a constant which only depends on $M(\beta)$.
<!-- end lem-16 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Fix $\omega\in{\mathsf{St}}_0$ and let $\omega_n:=\omega$, $\omega_i:=({\psi}_i^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ{\psi}_{n-1}^{-1})({\omega})$ ($0\leq i< n$). 
Discarding a set of measure zero, we may assume that $\omega_i$ do not hit the boundaries of the elements of the Markov partitions.  Fix $0\leq k\leq n-1$, and let $\widetilde{\omega}_k'$ be the lift of $\omega_k$ to ${\mathsf{St}}^\ast$ such that 
$\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_k(\widetilde{\omega}_k')=0$, then
$\widetilde{\omega}:=(\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ \cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_k)(\widetilde{\omega}_k')$ projects to $\omega$, and 
\begin{equation}\label{Eq-xi-tilde}
\widetilde{f}^{(n)}_{k+1}(\omega)=\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\widetilde{\psi}_k(\widetilde{\omega}_k')).
\end{equation}

Let $\widetilde{\gamma}$ denote the linear segment in the positive unstable direction $E^u_k$ from the bottom stable side of  $\widetilde{F}_k$ to $\widetilde{\omega}_k$. Then 
 $\widetilde{\Gamma}:=\widetilde{\psi}_k(\widetilde{\gamma})$  terminates at $\widetilde{\psi}_k(\widetilde{\omega})$, and starts on the bottom side of $D^{\tau_k}(\widetilde{F}_{k+1})$, where $\tau_k$, the ``twist"\index{Twist}, is a constant depending only on $k$ (through $\widetilde{\psi}_k$ and the direction of the  bottom side of $\widetilde{F}_k$, see  \S\ref{SSDriftZero}). So
\begin{equation}
\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\widetilde{\psi}_k(\widetilde{\omega}_k'))=\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\textrm{end}(\widetilde{\Gamma}))
-\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\textrm{beginning}(\widetilde{\Gamma}))+\tau_k.
\end{equation}

Let $\Gamma$ denote the projection of $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ to ${\mathsf{St}}_0$. 
Recall the notation for $\mathfrak P_k$ elements introduced in Lemma \ref{Lemma-Partition}, and
suppose $X^{(n)}_{k+1}(\omega)=Q^{k+1}_{\ell,m}$.  Then $\Gamma$ is the successive concatenation of the  linear segments
\begin{align*}
&\Gamma_1 = \textrm{ a $u$-fibre in $Q_{\ell,1}^{k+1}$}\\
&\Gamma_2 = \textrm{ a $u$-fibre in $Q_{\ell,2}^{k+1}$}\\
& \hspace{1cm}\cdots\cdots\cdots\\
&\Gamma_m=\textrm{ the beginning of a $u$-fibre in $Q_{\ell,m}^{k+1}$ which ends at $\psi_k(\omega_k)$.}
\end{align*}
Let ${\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}({\Gamma}_r):=\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\textrm{end}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_r))-\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\textrm{beginning}(\widetilde{\Gamma}_r))$ for some (any) lift of $\Gamma_r$. 
By the bounded geometry of ${F}_k$ and $F_{k+1}$, $|{\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}|\leq G_0(M)$, where $G_0(M)$ depends only on $M$, and  
                                                                                         
\begin{equation}\label{Eq-Sum-of Gains}
\widetilde{{\mathfrak{z}}}_{k+1}(\widetilde{\psi}_k(\widetilde{\omega}_k))=
\tau_k+\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}{\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}({\Gamma}_r).
\end{equation}
The sum ends at $k=m-1$, because ${\mathsf{Gain}}({\Gamma}_m)=0$.


 Recall that $\mathfrak P_{k+1}=\{Q^{k+1}_{1,1},\ldots,Q^{k+1}_{1,N_1}; Q^{k+1}_{2,1},\ldots,Q^{k+1}_{2,N_2}\}$, where $N_i=N_i(k+1)$. 

\medskip
\noindent
{\sc Claim:}
If  $\Gamma, \Gamma'$ are two $u$-fibres in $Q_{i,j}^{k+1}$, and 
  $j\neq N_1,N_2$, then 
${\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}(\Gamma)={\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}(\Gamma')$.


\medskip
\noindent
{\em Proof of the Claim:} Let $n=k+1$. Two $u$-fibres in $F_{n}$ have the same gain whenever  when we draw them in the plane as $u$-fibres in $\Pi(n)$ and  extend them a bit beyond their endpoints, they enter the same copy $g(\Pi(n))$, $g\in G$. This will happen whenever the endpoints of $\omega,\omega'$ are not separated by the beginning points of a $u$-fibre in $G(\Pi(n))$ which begins or passes through a singularity.

This is the case for all pairs of $u$-fibres in $Q_{i,j}^{k+1}$ whenever $1\leq j\leq N_i-1$.  The endpoints of such fibres cannot be separated by a singularity, because the top stable side of $Q_{i,j}^{k+1}$ does not contain a puncture when $j<N_i$ (if it did, $Q_i(k)$ would contain a puncture in its interior). And they  cannot be separated by the beginning point of a $u$-fibre which passes through a singularity, because $Q_{i,j+1}^{k+1}$ does not contain a puncture in its interior.  The claim follows.

\medskip
The claim guarantees that the quantity
$g_{k+1}(Q_{i,j}^{k+1}):={\mathsf{Gain}}_{k+1}(\Gamma)$  for some (all) $u$-fibres $\Gamma$ in $Q_{i,j}^{k+1}$,   
 is properly defined whenever  $j\neq N_1,N_2$ .  
Let $f_{k+1}:\mathfrak P_{k+1}\to\mathbb Z$, 
 $$\displaystyle f_{k+1}(Q_{i,j}^{k+1}):=\tau_k+\sum_{r=1}^{j-1}g_{k+1}(Q_{i,r}^{k+1}).$$
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                
               
                                                                                                                                  
                                                     
                                                                                                           
                                                        
             
By \eqref{Eq-xi-tilde} and \eqref{Eq-Sum-of Gains}, 
$\widetilde{f}^{(n)}_{k+1}(\omega)=f_{k+1}(X^{(n)}_{k+1}(\omega))$ a.e.


It remains to show that  $f_k$ are uniformly bounded. By definition, 
$|f_{k+1}(Q_{i,j}^{k+1})|\leq |\tau_k|+ j G_0(M)\leq  |\tau_k|+N_i(k+1) G_0(M)$, where 
$N_i(k+1)$ is the maximal number of times $\psi_k(Q_i(k))$ wraps around $F_{k+1}$. By the bounded geometry estimates on $F_k$ and the bounds on $\|d\psi_k\|$, $N_i(k+1)$ can be bounded by a constant depending only on $M(\beta)$. Similarly, $\tau_k$ can be bounded uniformly in terms of $M(\beta)$, because $N_0$ (the constant in \eqref{e.mat-prod-form}) can be bounded uniformly in terms of $M(\beta)$, and therefore  $\{\psi_i:i\geq 0\}$ is contained in a finite set, which depends only on $M(\beta)$.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lem-17: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Cylinders}
Suppose $a_i\in\mathfrak P_i$, then  
$\<a_{n-k},\ldots,\dot{a}_n,\ldots,a_{n+m}\>$ has non-empty interior iff $a_i\xrightarrow[]{\psi_i}a_{i+1}$ for all $i$. The interior is empty iff the Lebesgue measure is zero.
<!-- end lem-17 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
By \eqref{e.cylinder-shift}, it is sufficient to prove the lemma for $C=\<\dot{a}_n,a_{n+1},\ldots,a_{n+m}\>$.
 
Clearly, if $\mathrm{int}(C)\neq \varnothing$, then $a_i\xrightarrow[]{\psi_i}a_{i+1}$ for all $i$. 
The converse follows from  the properties of $\mathfrak P_i$ listed in Proposition \ref{Prop-Markov}, as in \cite{Adler-Weiss-MP}. Here are the details. 


 If $m=0$, $C=a_n$, and $\mathrm{int}(C)\neq \varnothing$.  Suppose by induction the lemma holds for $m-1$, and assume  $a_n\xrightarrow[]{\psi_n}a_{n+1}\xrightarrow[]{\psi_{n+1}}\cdots \xrightarrow[]{\psi_{n+m-1}}a_{n+m}$. By the induction hypothesis, there exists some point $\omega_{n+1}\in\mathrm{int}(C_{n+1})$, where  $C_{n+1}:=\<\dot{a}_{n+1},\ldots,a_{n+m}\>$. In addition, since $a_{n}\xrightarrow[]{\psi_{n}}a_{n+1}$, there is a point $\omega_n\in\mathrm{int}(a_{n})\cap\psi_n^{-1}(\mathrm{int}(a_{n+1}))$. By the Markov property, 
$$
\psi_{n}^{-1}[W^u(\psi_{n}(\omega_n),a_{n+1})]\subset W^u(\omega_n,a_{n}).
$$
By the product structure property, $\exists\omega^\ast\in W^u(\psi_{n}(\omega_n),a_{n+1})\cap W^s(\omega_{n+1},a_{n+1})$. 

We claim that $\omega\!\!:=\!\!\psi_{n}^{-1}(\omega^\ast)\!\!\in\!\! \mathrm{int}(C)$. First,   
$\omega\!\!\in\!\! \psi_{n}^{-1}[W^u(\psi_{n}(\omega_n),a_{n+1})]$, so by the Markov property, 
$\omega\in W^u(\omega_n,a_{n})\subset \mathrm{int}(a_n)$. 
Second, $\psi_{n}(\omega)\!\!\in\!\! W^s(\omega_{n+1}, a_{n+1})\!\!\subset\!\!\mathrm{int}(a_{n+1})$. Third,
by the Markov property  for every $n<j\leq n+m$,    
$$
(\psi_{j-1}\circ \cdots\circ \psi_{n})({\widetilde{\omega}})\!\!\in\!\! 
(\psi_{j-1}\circ \cdots\circ \psi_{n+1})[W^s(\omega_{n+1}, a_{n+1})]
\!\!\subset\!\! W^s((\psi_{j-1}\circ \cdots\circ \psi_{n+1})(\omega_{n+1}),a_{j})
\!\!\subset\!\! \mathrm{int}(a_{j}).
$$
Thus, $\displaystyle \omega\in \bigcap_{n<j\leq n+m}(\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1})(a_j)=\mathrm{int}(C)$. 
This proves the first part of the lemma. 

The second part is because cylinders are  convex.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lem-18: body_md -->
\label{Lemma-Cylinder-Area} Let  $C:=\<a_{n-k},\ldots,\dot{a}_n,\ldots,a_{n+m}\>\in\mathfrak C_{k,n,m}$. Then $C$ is an $(E^u_n,E^s_n)$-parallelogram in ${\mathsf{St}}_0$, and:  \index{Cylinders} \index{Stable side} \index{Unstable side}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
                                                                                
                                                                                                                                    
                                                                                                       
\item The stable side of $C$ has length $\ell^s(C)=\ell^s(a_{n-k})\cdot(\lambda^s_{n-k}\cdots \lambda^s_{n-1})$.
\item The unstable side of  $C$  has length $\ell^u(C)=\ell^u(a_{n+m})/(\lambda^u_{n}\cdots \lambda^u_{n+m-1})$.
\item $\mu_0(C)=\frac{1}{2}\ell^s(a_{n-k})\ell^u(a_{n+m})|\sin\measuredangle(E^s_{n},E^u_{n})|(\lambda^s_{n-k}\cdots\lambda^s_{n-1})/(\lambda^u_{n}\cdots \lambda^u_{n+m-1})$. 
\item The area of $C$ is bounded away from zero and infinity by constants which only depend on its length $k+m$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-18 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
First we consider  the case $k=0$. Set $\ell:=n+m$, and fix some  $C=\<\dot{a}_n,a_1,\ldots,a_\ell\>$ such that  $\mathrm{int}(C)\neq \varnothing$. By \eqref{e.cylinder}, $\displaystyle C=a_n\cap \bigcap_{j=n+1}^\ell (\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1})(a_j).$
Take $n+1\leq j\leq \ell$, then  $a_j\in\mathfrak P_j$ is an $(E^u_j,E^s_j)$-parallelogram, and $\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1}$ is an affine map which  maps $E^s_j, E^u_j$ to $E^s_n, E^u_n$. Thus $(\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1})(a_j)$ is an $(E^s_n,E^u_n)$-parallelogram. 
Passing to  the intersection over $j$, we see that $C$  is an $(E^s_n,E^u_n)$-parallelogram. 



Let us calculate its sides. 
Pick some ${\omega_n}\in\mathrm{int}(C)$, $n+1\leq j\leq \ell$, and let $\omega_j:=(\psi_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_n)(\omega_n)$.  By the Markov property, 
$$
(\psi_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_n)[W^s(\omega_n,a_n)]\subset W^s(\omega_j,a_j).
$$
Thus
$W^s(\omega_n,a_n)\subset a_n\cap\bigcap_{j=n+1}^{\ell}(\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1})(a_j)=C$. 
$W^s(\omega_n,a_n)$ is an open $s$-fiber in $a_n$. As such, it is an $E^s_n$-segment of length $\ell^s(a_n)$.
It follows that  the stable side of $C$ has length $\ell^s(C)\geq \ell^s(a_n)$. Since $C\subset a_n$,  $\ell^s(C)=\ell^s(a_n)$.

Let $W:=(\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{\ell-1}^{-1})(W^u(\omega_\ell,a_\ell))$. By the Markov property, for all $n+1\leq j\leq \ell$,   
$$
(\psi_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_n)(W)=(\psi_j^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{\ell-1}^{-1})(W^u(\omega_\ell,a_\ell))\subset W^u(\omega_j,a_j)\subset a_j.
$$
So $\displaystyle W\subset  \bigcap_{j=n+1}^{\ell}(\psi_n^{-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{j-1}^{-1})(a_j)=C$. 
$W^u(\omega_\ell,a_\ell)$ is an open $u$-fiber in $a_\ell$. As such, it is an $E^u_\ell$-segment of length $\ell^u(a_\ell)$.
