By construction, $\mathrm{int}(I_{N',j})\cap K({\varepsilon})$ is a finite disjoint union of  intervals $\mathrm{int}(I_{N'+1,j'})$.  By the  maximality of $N'$, the one whose closure contains an endpoint of $J$ does not cover $J\cap K({\varepsilon})$. Necessarily, another one, say $I_{N'+1,j'}$ is completely contained in $\overline{J}$. 
By \eqref{e.rho-eps}, 
 $|I_{N'+1,j'}|\geq \rho |I_{N',j}|$, whence $|J|\geq \rho |I_{N',j}|$. 

In summary, 
$
\nu(I)=\nu(\overline{J}\cap \overline{K(\xi)})\leq 2\nu(\overline{I_{N',j}})\leq 2C_0|I_{N',j}|^{1-s}
\leq 2C_0(\rho^{-1}|J|)^{1-s}
$. Since $J\subset \overline{I}$, $\nu(I)\leq 2C_0\rho^{-(1-s)}|I|^{1-s}$. 

\medskip
\noindent
{\em Case 2.\/} $J\subset \overline{I_{n_0,j}}$.

Let $n\geq n_0$ be the maximal integer such that  $J\subset \overline{I_{n,j}}$ for some $j$. Then there are $\ell_1,\ell_2$ such that $\overline{I_{n,j,\ell_i}}$ cover some endpoint of $J$, and their other endpoint is inside the interior of $J$. 

If $\overline{J}\subset \overline{I_{n,j,\ell_1}}\cup  \overline{I_{n,j,\ell_2}}$, then we continue as in Case 1.
Otherwise, there is some $\ell_3$ such that $I_{n,j,\ell_3}\subset J$, and $\rho|I_{n,j}|\leq |I_{n,j,\ell_3}|\leq |J|$  by \eqref{e.rho-eps}. Recalling that $J\subset \overline{I}_{n,j}$ we obtain that for all $s>c\xi^2/{\varepsilon}$
$$
\nu(I)=\nu(J)\leq \nu(I_{n,j})\leq C_0|I_{n,j}|^{1-s}\leq C_0 \rho^{-(1-s)}|J|^{1-s}\leq C_0 \rho^{-(1-s)}|I|^{1-s}.
$$
This completes the proof that \eqref{e.mass-dist} holds for each $s>c\xi^2/{\varepsilon}$. 

By Frostman's lemma, ${\mathrm{HD}}(W\cap K(\xi))\geq 1-c\xi^2/{\varepsilon}$.
<!-- end proof-88 -->
<!-- head-18: body_md -->
First we cover ${\mathsf{St}}^\ast$ be a countable collection of  $(E^s_0,E^u_0)$-parallelograms $Q_i$.  Then ${\mathrm{HD}}(\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))=\sup_i {\mathrm{HD}}(\mathsf{Gen}(\xi)\cap Q_i)$, and it is sufficient to show that there are constants $c_1,c_2, \xi_0$ such that for every $i$ and $|\xi|<\xi_0$,  
$$
1-c_1\xi^2\leq {\mathrm{HD}}(\mathsf{Gen}(\xi)\cap Q_i)\leq 1-c_2\xi^2.
$$

We fix $i$, set $Q:=Q_i$, and denote the $E^u_0$-side of $Q$ by $W$. 

Let $\vartheta_{Q}:Q\to W$ be the projection along the $E^s_0$-direction.
If $\vartheta_{Q}({\widetilde{\omega}}_1)=\vartheta_Q({\widetilde{\omega}}_2)$, 
then the linear segment $J_{{\widetilde{\omega}}_1,{\widetilde{\omega}}_2}$ from ${\widetilde{\omega}}_1$ to ${\widetilde{\omega}}_2$  is parallel to $E^s_0$, therefore 
$$
{\rm dist}((\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0)({\widetilde{\omega}}_1),(\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0)({\widetilde{\omega}}_2))\leq {\rm diam}[(\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0)(J_{{\widetilde{\omega}}_1,{\widetilde{\omega}}_2})]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0.
$$
It follows that $|z_{nN_0}({\widetilde{\omega}}_1)-z_{nN_0}({\widetilde{\omega}}_2)|=O(1)$. 
By Lemma \ref{l.solution-xi} and Proposition \ref{p.Pressure-and-Geometric-Pressure}, for any sequence of integers $N_k\uparrow\infty$, if 
$
\exists \eta_{N_k}\to\eta$ s.t. $\mathcal P_{N_k}'(\eta_{n_k})=z_{N_k}({\widetilde{\omega}}_1)$, then $\exists \eta_{N_k}'\to\eta$ s.t.  $\mathcal P_{N_k}'(\eta_{N_k}')=z_{N_k}({\widetilde{\omega}}_2)$, and vice versa.
It follows that  ${\widetilde{\omega}}_1$  is $\mu_\xi$-generic iff ${\widetilde{\omega}}_2$ is $\mu_\xi$-generic.
Thus, $\mathsf{Gen}(\xi)\cap Q=\vartheta_Q^{-1}(W\cap\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))$.  

Since $\vartheta_Q^{-1}(W\cap\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))$  is a bi-Lipschitz image of $(W\cap\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))\times [0,1]$
$$
{\mathrm{HD}}\big[\mathsf{Gen}(\xi)\cap Q\big]={\mathrm{HD}}\big[(W\cap\mathsf{Gen}(\xi))\times [0,1]\big]={\mathrm{HD}}\big[W\cap\mathsf{Gen}(\xi)\big]+1.
$$
Now the theorem follows directly from Lemmas \ref{LmHDUpper} and \ref{LmHDLower}.
\hfill$\square$
<!-- end head-18 -->
<!-- head-19: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf{Gen}$ denote the set of ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ which are generic for some locally finite ergodic invariant measure. The theorem states that $\mathsf{NonGen}:={\mathsf{St}}^\ast\setminus\mathsf{Gen}$ is a residual set, with  zero Lebesgue measure and full Hausdorff dimension. 

\medskip
\noindent
{\bf Residual:} Recall the definition of $\overline{S}_n({\widetilde{\omega}})$ from the proof of Lemma \ref{LmHDUpper}.  
Fix $\xi>0$ and let
$
E_{n_0}(\xi)=\{{\widetilde{\omega}}: \exists n\geq n_0 \textrm{ such that }\overline{S}_n({\widetilde{\omega}})=[\mathsf{P}_n'(\xi)]\}.
$

 $\displaystyle \mathsf{NonGen}\supset \bigcap_{n_0} \mathrm{int}\left[ E_{n_0}(\xi/2) \cap E_{n_0}(\xi) \right]$, because as shown in the proof of Lemma \ref{LmHDUpper},  if ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is in the right-hand-side, then $\exists n_k, n_k'\uparrow\infty$ and $\xi_{n_k}\to\xi$, $\xi_{n_k'}\to\xi/2$ such that $\mathsf{P}_{n_k}'(\xi_{n_k})=z_{n_kN_0}({\widetilde{\omega}})+O(1)$ and $\mathsf{P}_{n_k'}'(\xi_{n_k}')=z_{n_k'N_0}({\widetilde{\omega}})+O(1)$, and this implies that ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ has at least two different historical measures, $\mu_{\xi}$ and $\mu_{\xi/2}$. 


The set $\mathrm{int}\left[ E_{n_0}(\xi/2) \cap E_{n_0}(\xi) \right]$ is clearly open. 

We claim that it is also dense. It  
suffices to show that every cylinder $\<\dot{a}_0,\ldots,a_n\>$ has an extension  $\<\dot{a}_0,\ldots,a_{n+m+\ell}\>$ where 
$$\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n+m} f_j(a_i)=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m}'(\xi/2)]\textrm{ and }
\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n+m+\ell} f_j(a_i)=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m+\ell}'(\xi)].$$

Let $S_i^j:=f_i(X_i)+\cdots+ f_j(X_j)$. By the local limit theorem {for large deviations (Theorem \ref{ThLD})}, 
$$
{\mathbb{P}}\left[ S_n^{n+m}=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m}'(\xi/2)]-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} f_j(a_j) \bigg|X_n=a_n\right]\neq 0\textrm{ for all $m$ large enough}. 
$$
Fix $m$ like that. The event on the right is a union of non-empty cylinders $\<\dot{a}_0,\ldots,a_{n+m}\>$ such that 
$\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n+m} f_j(a_j)=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m}'(\xi/2)]$. 
Fix one of these cylinders, then again, 
$$
{\mathbb{P}}\left[ S_{n+m}^{n+m+\ell}=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m+\ell}'(\xi)]-\sum_{j=1}^{n+m-1} f_j(a_j) \bigg|X_{n+m}=a_{n+m}\right]\neq 0\textrm{ for all $\ell$ large enough}.  
$$
Fix $m$ like that, then the event on the right is a union of cylinders  $\<\dot{a}_0,\ldots,a_{n+m+\ell}\>\neq \varnothing$ such that  $\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n+m+\ell} f_j(a_i)=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m}'(\xi)]$ and 
$\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^{n+m} f_j(a_i)=[\mathsf{P}_{n+m}'(\xi/2)]$.

In summary, $\mathsf{NonGen}$ contains a dense $G_\delta$ set. It follows that it is residual.

\medskip
\noindent
{\bf Zero Lebesgue Measure:} This is obvious since $\mu_0$ is proportional to the Lebesgue measure, and $\mu_0$-a.e. ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ is $\mu_0$-generic, by the ratio ergodic theorem.

\medskip
\noindent
{\bf Full Hausdorff Dimension:} 
Fix $C, \widehat n_0>0$ such that 
$$|\mathsf{P}_n'(0)|=|\mathbb E(S_n)|\leq C\textrm{ and  }C^{-1}n\leq \mathsf{P}_n''\leq Cn\textrm{ on $[-1,1]$ for all $n>\widehat n_0$,}
$$ see \eqref{Pres1stDer}, \eqref{Pres2dDer} and Proposition \ref{Prop-Var-Growth}. 

By Lemma \ref{l.delta-pressure-is-uni-conv}, there are $c, \widehat n_1>0$  such that for all $k,n\geq \widehat n_1$ and $|\xi|\leq 1$,
$$
c^{-1}n\leq \mathrm{Var}(S_{k+n}-S_k)\leq c n\textrm{ and } c^{-1}n\leq\mathsf{P}_{k+n}''(\xi)-\mathsf{P}_k''(\xi)\leq c n.
$$

                                                                                                                                                                                                     
                                       
                          
                                     
                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
                
                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
              
                                                  


\noindent
Let $K:=(C+c+1)(c+1)$. Fix  $0<\xi<1$ and choose an integer 
$$
L>\max\left\{\widehat n_0, \widehat n_1, \frac{2(C+1)K}{\xi}, \frac{2Cc}{1-\xi} \right\}.
$$
Let $n_i:=4^i$, and
define $\xi_{n_i L}:=\frac{\xi}{2K}$ for $i$ odd, $\xi_{n_i L}:=\frac{\xi}{K}$ for $i$ even, and extend by linear interpolation
$$
\displaystyle \xi_{n}:=\frac{n-n_iL}{n_{i+1}L-n_iL}\xi_{n_{i+1}L}+\frac{n_{i+1}L-n}{n_{i+1}L-n_iL}\xi_{n_{i}L}\ \ (n_i L\leq n\leq n_{i+1}L).
$$
Obviously, $|\xi_n|\leq \frac{1}{K}<1$ for all $n$. We claim that if $n>4$ then 
$$
|\xi_{nL}-\xi_{(n-1)L}|<\frac{\xi}{Kn}.
$$
To see this, let  $i$ be the integer such that $n-1\in [n_i,n_{i+1}-1]$. Then  $(n-1)L, nL\in [n_iL,n_{i+1}L]$, and therefore   
$
|\xi_{nL}-\xi_{(n-1)L}|=\frac{|\xi_{n_{i+1}L}-\xi_{n_{i}L}|}{n_{i+1}-n_i}=\frac{\xi/(2K)}{(3/4)n_{i+1}}<\xi/(Kn).
$



Let $z_n:=[\mathsf{P}_n'(\xi_n)]$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item  $z_{n_i L}:=[\mathsf{P}_{n_i L}'(\xi)]$ for $i$ even;
\item  $z_{n_i L}:=[\mathsf{P}_{n_i L}'(\xi/2)]$ for $i$ odd.
\end{enumerate}
In addition, we claim that 
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item[(c)]   $ |z_{nL}-z_{(n-1)L}|\leq \xi \mathrm{Var}(S_{nL}-S_{(n-1)L})$ for all $n$;
\item[(d)]  $\exists\eta_{nL}\in [-1,1]$ such that  $z_{nL}-z_{(n-1)L}=\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(\eta_{nL})-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\eta_{nL})$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end head-19 -->
<!-- head-20: body_md -->
$|z_n-\mathsf{P}_n'(\xi_n)|\leq 1$, therefore
\begin{align*}
&|z_{nL}-z_{(n-1)L}|\leq \bigl|\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(\xi_{nL})-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{(n-1)L})\bigr|+2\\
&\leq \bigl|\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(\xi_{nL})-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{nL})\bigr|+\bigl|\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{nL})-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{(n-1)L})\bigr|+2\\
&\leq \left(\bigl|\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(\eta)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\eta)\bigr]^{\eta=\xi_{nL}}_{\eta=0}\bigr|\!+\!|\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(0)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(0)|\right)\\
&\hspace{7cm}+\!\bigl|\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{nL})\!-
\!\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(\xi_{(n-1)L})\bigr|\!+\!2\\
&\leq \max_{[-1,1]}(\mathsf{P}_{nL}''-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'')\cdot |\xi_{nL}|+2C+(\max_{[-1,1]}\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'')\cdot|\xi_{nL}-\xi_{(n-1)L}|+2\\
&\leq c L(\xi/K)+2C+C(n-1)L\cdot \xi/(Kn)+2<L\xi\left(\frac{c+C}{K}+\frac{2(C+1)K}{K L\xi}\right)\\
&<c^{-1} L\xi \leq \xi{\rm Var}(S_{nL}-S_{(n-1)L})\ \ \textrm{ by choice of $L$, $K$ and  $c$}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end head-20 -->
<!-- head-21: body_md -->
By the previous calculations, $|z_{nL}-z_{(n-1)L}|<c^{-1}\xi L$. At the same time, 
\begin{align*}
\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(1)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(1)&\geq \mathsf{P}_{nL}'(0)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(0)+\min_{[-1,1]}(\mathsf{P}_{nL}''-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'')\cdot(1-0)\\
&\geq -2C+c^{-1}L=c^{-1}L\xi +(c^{-1}L(1-\xi)-2C)\geq c^{-1}L\xi.\\
\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(-1)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(-1)&\leq \mathsf{P}_{nL}'(0)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(0)+\min_{[-1,1]}(\mathsf{P}_{nL}''-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'')\cdot(-1-0)\\
&\leq 2C-c^{-1}L=-c^{-1}L\xi -(c^{-1}L(1-\xi)-2C)\leq -c^{-1}L\xi.
\end{align*}
So $z_{nL}-z_{(n-1)L}$ lies between $\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(-1)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(-1)$ and $\mathsf{P}_{nL}'(1)-\mathsf{P}_{(n-1)L}'(1)$. Part (d) follows from the intermediate value theorem. 


Let $K(\xi)=\{{\widetilde{\omega}}: \overline{S}_{nL}({\widetilde{\omega}})=z_{nL}$ for all $n\}$. Every ${\widetilde{\omega}}$ in $K$ has at least two different historical measures, and is therefore in $\mathsf{NonGen}$. 
Property (d) allows us to push through the  proof of Lemmas \ref{l.LLT-LD-Blocks} and \ref{LmHDLower}, and  deduce  that ${\mathrm{HD}}(K(\xi))\geq 1-O(\xi^2)$.
Thus ${\mathrm{HD}}(\mathsf{NonGen})\geq {\mathrm{HD}}(K(\xi))+1\geq 
2-O(\xi^2)\xrightarrow[\xi\to 0]{}2$.\hfill$\square$
<!-- end head-21 -->
<!-- lem-61: body_md -->
\label{l.v-contracts}
For every $a,b\in 2\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, $|(v_a\circ v_b)'|\leq 1$ on $[-1,1]$. If $(a,b)\neq (\pm 2,\mp2)$, then $|(v_a\circ v_b)'|\leq \frac{1}{9}$ on $[-1,1]$.
<!-- end lem-61 -->
<!-- proof-89: body_md -->
$(v_a\circ v_b)(t)={\tiny \left(
\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & a
\end{array}
\right)\left(\begin{array}{cc}
0 & 1 \\
1 & b
\end{array}
\right)\cdot t=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1 & b \\
a & ab+1
\end{array}
\right)}\cdot t=\frac{t+b}{at+ab+1}$, so
$$
(v_a\circ v_b)'(t)=\frac{1}{(at+ab+1)^2}.
$$
Suppose $|t|\leq 1$.

\noindent
$\bullet$ 
If $(a,b)=(2,-2)$, then
$
\displaystyle |(v_a\circ v_b)'(t)|{=}\frac{1}{(2t-3)^2}\leq 1
$.
 
\noindent
$\bullet$  
 If $(a,b)=(-2,2)$, then
$
\displaystyle |(v_a\circ v_b)'(t)|{=} \frac{1}{(-2t-3)^2}\leq 1
$.

\noindent
$\bullet$ 
  If $(a,b)=\pm (2,2)$ then
$
\displaystyle |(v_a\circ v_b)'(t)|\leq \frac{1}{(5-2|t|)^2}\leq \frac{1}{9}.$

\noindent
$\bullet$ 
In all other cases $|ab|\geq 8$ and $|ab|>|at|+1$, so \\
$\displaystyle
|(v_a\circ v_b)'(t)|\leq \frac{1}{(|ab|-|a|-1)^2}\leq \frac{1}{(|ab|-\frac{1}{2}|ab|-1)^2}\leq \frac{1}{(4-1)^2}=\frac{1}{9}.
$
<!-- end proof-89 -->
<!-- lem-62: body_md -->
\label{l.limit-cfe-exists}
The limit \eqref{e.ecfe} exists for all $m_i\in 2\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, and belongs to $[-1,1]$.
<!-- end lem-62 -->
<!-- proof-90: body_md -->
Suppose the sequence of $2m_i$ does not terminate in an infinite sequence of the form $(2,-2,2,-2,\cdots)$, then
the intervals $(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_N})[-1,1]$ form a decreasing sequence of intervals with diameter tending to zero. So
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots,2m_n]=\lim_{n\to\infty}(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_n})(0)\textrm{ exists, and belongs to }[-1,1].
$$

Next, suppose  $2m_i$ does terminate in an infinite sequence of the form $(2,-2,2,-2,\ldots)$.
Assume first that  $(2m_1,2m_2,\ldots)$ equals $(2,-2,2,-2,\ldots)$. For $i$ odd,
$$
(v_{2m_i}\circ v_{2m_{i+1}})(x)=\frac{x-2}{2x-3}=\biggl(\begin{array}{ll}
1 & -2\\
2 & -3
\end{array}\biggr)\cdot x.
$$
The is a parabolic M\"obius transformation, therefore for all $\xi\in\mathbb R$, $(v_{2m_i}\circ v_{2m_{i+1}})^N(\xi)$ converges to the unique fixed point in $\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}$, equal to $1$, uniformly on compact subsets of 
$[-1,1]$. Let $\xi_n:=0$ for $n$ even and $\xi_n:=v_2(0)=\frac{1}{2}$ for $n$ odd, then 
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots,2m_{2n}]=\lim_{n\to\infty}(v_{2m_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2m_n})(0)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\biggl(\begin{array}{ll}
1 & -2\\
2 & -3
\end{array}\biggr)^n\cdot \xi_n=1.
$$
The case when $(m_1,m_2,\ldots)$ terminates with $(2,-2,2,-2,\cdots)$ easily follows.
<!-- end proof-90 -->
<!-- lem-63: body_md -->
\label{l.f-expansion}
Every $\alpha\in (-1,1)\setminus\mathbb Q$ admits a unique sequence of $m_i\in \mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ such that
$\alpha=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$.\index{Even continued fraction expansion!existence and uniqueness}
<!-- end lem-63 -->
<!-- proof-91: body_md -->
By the previous lemma,  for every sequence $n_i\in 2\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$,
$
-1\leq [0;n_1,n_2,\cdots]\leq 1.
$
The maximum is obtained at $t:=[0;2,-2,2,-2,\ldots]$ and the minimum is obtained at $s:=[0;-2,2,-2,\ldots]$. Since $t=[0;2,-2,t]$, $t=1$. Since $s=[0;-2,2,s]$, $s=-1$.

Recall the  {\em even Gauss map}  $E:(-1,1)\to (-1,1)$ from \eqref{EvenGauss}.
        
                 
            
                                                                                                     
               
Suppose $\alpha\in (-1,1)\setminus\mathbb Q$. Set $r_0:=\alpha$, $m_0=0$,
$r_n:=E^n(\alpha)$, and let $m_n\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ be the unique integer such that $\frac{1}{r_n}\in 2m_{n+1}+(-1,1).$
Starting from the identity $\displaystyle r_{n+1}=\frac{1}{r_n}-2m_{n+1}$, we find that
\begin{align*}
r_n&=\frac{1}{2m_{n+1}+r_{n+1}}=\left[0;2m_{n+1},\frac{1}{r_{n+1}}\right]\\
r_{n-1}&=\frac{1}{2m_{n}+r_{n}}=\cfrac{1}{2m_{n}+\cfrac{1}{2m_{n+1}+r_{n+1}}}=\left[0;2m_{n},2m_{n+1},
\frac{1}{r_{n+1}}\right]\\
&\cdots\cdots\cdots\cdots\\
r_1&=\left[0;2m_2,2m_3,\cdots,2m_{n+1},\frac{1}{r_{n+1}}\right]\\
\alpha&=r_0=\frac{1}{2m_1+r_1}=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots,2m_{n+1},\frac{1}{r_{n+1}}].
\end{align*}
 Looking at Lemma \ref{l.limit-cfe-exists} and its proof, we deduce that the last expression tends to $[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$. Therefore $\alpha=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\cdots]$.
This is the even CFE of $\alpha$.


Next we show that the even CFE is unique. Suppose $\alpha=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$ and $\alpha$ is irrational. Then
$
\frac{1}{\alpha}=2m_1+[0;2m_2,2m_3,\ldots]\in 2m_1+(-1,1)
$
This determines $m_1$ uniquely, and we see that $E(\alpha)=\frac{1}{\alpha}-2m_1=[0;2m_2,2m_3,\ldots]$, so 
$
\frac{1}{E(\alpha)}=2m_2+[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]\in 2m_2+(-1,1).
$
This determines $m_2$ uniquely, and shows that $E^2(\alpha)=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]$.   Continuing in this way we see that each $m_n$ is uniquely determined by the condition $\frac{1}{E^{n-1}(\alpha)}\in 2m_n+(-1,1)$.
<!-- end proof-91 -->
<!-- lem-64: body_md -->
\label{l.BT-bounded-pm-two}
An irrational number\index{Even continued fraction expansion!of numbers of bounded type}
 $\alpha$ is of bounded type iff the even continued fraction expansion of $\alpha$ is uniformly bounded, 
 and  the lengths of the sunwards $(2,-2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ appearing in the even CFE of $\alpha$ are bounded.  Moreover, if 
\begin{align}
B(\alpha):=& \sup\{\textrm{partial quotients of the regular CFE of $\alpha$}\}\notag\\
M_1(\alpha):=&\sup\{\textrm{absolute values of partial quotients of the even CFE of $\alpha$}\}\notag\\
M_2(\beta):=&\sup\{\textrm{length of the sub-words $(2,-2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ or $(-2,2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ }\notag\\
&\hspace{6cm}\textrm{ which appear in the even CFE of $\alpha$}\}\notag\\
M(\alpha):=&\max\{M_1(\alpha),M_2(\alpha)\}+1.
\end{align}
 Then $M(\alpha)\geq 3$ and 
 $B(\alpha)-3\leq M(\alpha)\leq B(\alpha)+3$.
<!-- end lem-64 -->
<!-- proof-92: body_md -->
$M(\alpha)\geq 3$ because $M_1(\alpha)\geq 2$.

The qualitative part of the lemma asserting that $M(\alpha)$ is finite iff $B(\alpha)$ is finite  has short geometric proof, relying on the well-known relation between the regular (resp. even) CFEs of $\alpha$ and the dynamical properties of projection of a geodesic ray in $\mathbb H$ with endpoint $\alpha$ to $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\setminus\mathbb H$ (resp. $\Gamma(2)\setminus\mathbb H$):
Let $\alpha:=[2m_{0};2m_{1},2m_{2},\ldots]$ be the even CFE of $\alpha$.  $M(\alpha)=\infty$ iff   any geodesic $\gamma$ on $\mathbb H$ which terminates at $\alpha$ projects to a geodesic $\Gamma(2)\gamma$ on $\Gamma(2)\setminus\mathbb H$ which enters at least one of the cusps of $\Gamma(2)\setminus\mathbb H$ arbitrarily deeply.
Since $\Gamma(2)\lhd \mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)$, the surface $\Gamma(2)\setminus\mathbb H$ is a  regular cover of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\setminus\mathbb H$. Necessarily, $M(\alpha)=\infty$ iff  $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb Z)\gamma$ enters the cusp of the modular surface arbitrarily deeply. This happens iff  $B(\alpha)=\infty$.\index{Kraaikamp-Lopes theorem}


Next we give another proof, which yields the stronger quantitative assertion that $B(\alpha)-3\leq M(\alpha)\leq B(\alpha)+3$.  The proof relies on  a procedure due to Kraaikamp \cite{Kraaikamp}, as presented in \cite{Kraaikamp-Lopes}, which  transforms the regular CFE to the even CFE.\footnote{\cite{Kraaikamp-Lopes} use a different definition for the even CFE which results in a different (though equivalent) expansion. What follows is  translation to our language.}  

Kraaikamp's procedure is based on the following algebraic identities \cite{Kraaikamp,Kraaikamp-Lopes}:
	\begin{enumerate}[(S1)]
		\item $[A,1,B,z]=[A+1,-(B+1), -z]$
		\item $[A,B,z]=[A+1,-1,-(B-1),-z]$
		\item $[A,B,z]=[A-1,1,-(B+1),-z]$
	\end{enumerate}	
To verify these identities, we first check by direct calculation that
	$$
	\left(\begin{array}{cc}
		1 & a \\
		0 & 1
	\end{array}
	\right)\left(\begin{array}{cc}
		0 & {\varepsilon} \\
		1 & 1
	\end{array}
	\right)\left(\begin{array}{cc}
		0 & 1 \\
		1 & b
	\end{array}
	\right)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
		1 & a+{\varepsilon} \\
		0 & 1
	\end{array}
	\right)\left(\begin{array}{cc}
		0 & -{\varepsilon} \\
		1 & b+1
	\end{array}
	\right).
	$$
	Now suppose  ${\varepsilon}=\pm 1$, and let us replace each matrix by the M\"obius transformation it defines. Applying the M\"obius transformations on the two sides of the equation to $1/z$, and noting that ${\varepsilon}^{-1}={\varepsilon}$, we obtain
$		[a;{\varepsilon},{\varepsilon} b,{\varepsilon} z]=[a+{\varepsilon};-{\varepsilon}(b+1),-{\varepsilon} z].$

	Substituting ${\varepsilon}=1$, $a=A$, $b=B$, gives (S1).
	Substituting ${\varepsilon}=-1$, $a=A+1$, $b=B-1$, gives (S2).
	Substituting ${\varepsilon}=1$, $a=A-1$, $b=-(B+1)$, $z=-w$ gives (S3).
	
	
	Suppose now that $\alpha$ has regular CFE
	$
	\alpha=[B_0;B_1,B_2,\ldots]
	$, i.e. $B_0\in\mathbb Z$ and $B_i\in\mathbb N$. If all partial quotients $B_i$ are even, this is also the even CFE, and the lemma is trivial. If not, choose the minimal $n\geq 0$ such that   $B_0,\ldots,B_{n-1}$ are even and $B_n$ is odd.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\em Case 1.\/}  $B_{n+1}=1$. Write using (S1)
	\begin{align*}
		\alpha&=[\underset{\textrm{even}}{\underbrace{B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1}}},\underset{\textrm{odd}}{\underbrace{B_n}},1,B_{n+2},z],\textrm{ where }z:=[B_{n+3};B_{n+4},\ldots]\\
		&=[\underset{\textrm{even}}{\underbrace{B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1}}},\underset{\textrm{even}}{\underbrace{B_n+1}},-(B_{n+2}+1),-z],
	\end{align*}
and we have gained one additional even digit.

\smallskip
\noindent
{\em Case 2.\/}  $B_{n+1}>1$. In this case we write
	\begin{align*}
		\alpha&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		\big[B_n;B_{n+1},z\big]\big],\textrm{ where }z:=[B_{n+2};B_{n+3},\ldots]\\
		&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		[B_n+1;-1,-(B_{n+1}-1),-z]\big], \textrm{ by (S2)}\\
		&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		B_n+1,[-1;-(B_{n+1}-1),-z]\big] \textrm{ trivially}\\
		&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		B_n+1,[-2;1,B_{n+1}-2,z]\big],\textrm{ by (S3)}\\
		&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		B_n+1,-2,[1,B_{n+1}-2,z]\big],\textrm{ trivially}\\
				&=\big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		B_n+1,-2,[2,-1,-(B_{n+1}-3),-z]\big],\textrm{ by (S2)}\\
				&= \big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},
		B_n+1,-2,2,-[1;(B_{n+1}-3),z]\big]\\
               
                 
		& \hspace{5cm}\cdots\cdots\cdots  \textrm{ (repeated applications of last two steps)}\\
		&= \big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},B_n+1,
		\underset{B_{n+1}-2}{\underbrace{-2,2,-2,\cdots,(-1)^{B_{n+1}}2}},(-1)^{B_{n+1}+1}[1;1,z]\big].
	\end{align*}
	Write $[1;1,z]=[1;1,B_{n+2},w]$ with $w=[B_{n+3};B_{n+4},\ldots]$. By (S1),  
	$$[1;1,B_{n+2},w]=[2;-(B_{n+2}+1),-w]=[2;-[B_{n+2}+1,w]].$$
	Substituting this in the above leads to
	\begin{align*}
		\alpha&= \big[B_0;B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1},B_n+1,
		\underset{B_{n+1}-1}{\underbrace{-2,2,-2,\cdots,(-1)^{B_{n+1}+1}2}},\\
		&\hspace{4.9cm}(-1)^{B_{n+1}}[B_{n+2}+1;
		B_{n+3},B_{n+4},\ldots]\big].
	\end{align*}
	This representation starts with at least $n+B_{n+1}>n$ even digits.
	
\smallskip
\noindent
	In both cases the initial CFE starts with $n$ even digits,  and the final CFE starts with at least $n+1$ even digits. The new expansion may contain a stretch of $(2,-2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ of  length bounded by
	$
	M:=\max\{B_i:i\geq 0\}.
	$	
	Finally, the two expansions agree with each other on the  first $n$ digits.
	
	Proceeding by induction, we obtain an infinite sequences $C_i$ and $w_i\in (-1,1)$ s.t.
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item $\alpha=[C_0;C_1,\ldots,C_n,w_n]$,  and $|w_n|$ is uniformly bounded;
		\item  $C_i\leq M+1$, $C_i$ are all even, and if $i\neq 0$ , then $C_i\neq 0$;
		\item All sub-words  $(-2,2,-2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ of  $(C_0,C_1,C_2\ldots)$ have length less than $M$.
	\end{enumerate}
Looking at the proof of Lemma \ref{l.limit-cfe-exists}, it is easy to verify that
	$
	\alpha=[C_0;C_0,C_1,\ldots]
	$.  

Looking closer 	at the previous procedure we see that it either modifies a digit by  $+1$ or a sign or both at most  twice, or it replaces a digit $B$ by a word of the form $\pm (-2,2,\ldots,\pm 2)$ of length $\leq B
+2$. It follows that $B(\alpha)-3\leq M(\alpha)\leq B(\alpha)+3$.
<!-- end proof-92 -->
<!-- lem-65: body_md -->
\label{l.BT-compact}
For every $M>1$ there is a compact subset $K\subset (-1,1)$ as follows. Suppose $M(\beta)\leq M$ and the even CFE of
$\beta$ is $\beta=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$. Then
$$ r_k:=[0;2m_k;2m_{k+1},\ldots]\in K\textrm{ for all }k.$$
<!-- end lem-65 -->
<!-- proof-93: body_md -->
$\displaystyle
\pm \frac{1}{r_k}\in \bigcup_{n=1}^{M} \underset{m\neq -1}{\bigcup_{0<|m|\leq M}}(\underset{n\textrm{ even (incl. zero)} }{\underbrace{v_{2}v_{-2}\cdots v_{-2}}})\circ (v_2 v_{2m})([-1,1]) $
$$\hspace{-1cm}\bigcup \bigcup_{n=1}^M \underset{m\neq 1}{\bigcup_{0<|m|\leq M}}(\underset{n\textrm{ odd } }{\underbrace{v_{2}v_{-2}\cdots v_{2}}})\circ (v_{-2} v_{2m})([-1,1])\bigcup \bigcup_{2\leq m\leq M} v_{2m}[-1,1].
$$
The first and second  sets take care of $1/r_k=[2;\ast,\ast,\ldots]$, the third set takes care of $1/r_k=[2m;\ast,\ast,\ldots]$ where $2m>2$, and the plus/minus in front of $1/r_k$ takes care of the remaining (symmetric) options.

Call the set on the right-hand-side $K'$.
We claim that $K'$ is a finite union of compact subsets of $(-1,1)$. In what follows, $\mathrm{Int}[c,d]$ is the closed interval with endpoints $c,d$ (even if $c>d$).
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\item $v_2v_{2m}[-1,1]=v_2[\frac{1}{2m+1},\frac{1}{2m-1}]=\mathrm{Int}[\frac{2m+1}{4m+3},\frac{2m-1}{4m-1}]$. We know that $v_a:[-1,1]\hookrightarrow[-1,1]$ are continuous homeomorphisms onto their images.  If $m\neq -1$, then $\pm 1$ is not in the interval $\mathrm{Int}[\frac{2m+1}{4m+3},\frac{2m-1}{4m-3}]$. So
    $\displaystyle
    v_2v_{2m}[-1,1]$ is a compact subset of $(-1,1).
    $
    
    Similarly, $v_2v_{-2}\cdots v_{-2}:[-1,1]\hookrightarrow[-1,1]$ is a homeomorphisms onto its image. As such, it must map a compact subset of $(-1,1)$ onto a compact subset of $(-1,1)$. This takes care of the first union of sets.
\item The second union of sets can be handled in the same way, using the observation that $(v_{-2}v_{2m})[-1,1]=\mathrm{Int}[\frac{2m+1}{-4m-1},\frac{2m-1}{-4m+3}]$ does not contain $\pm 1$, when $m\neq 1$.
\item The third union of sets obviously does not contain $\pm 1$, and is compact.
\end{enumerate}
Since $K'$ is a finite union of compact subsets of $(-1,1)$, it too is a compact subset of $(-1,1)$. The lemma follows with $K:= K'\cup(-K')$.
<!-- end proof-93 -->
<!-- head-22: body_md -->
{\em  For every $M>1$, $0<\varepsilon<1$ there exists $T$ as follows: If  $r\in{\mathsf{BT}}(M)$,  
   then every line with slope $r$ and length $T$ on ${\mathsf{St}}_0$ is $\varepsilon$-dense in ${\mathsf{St}}_0$.}
<!-- end head-22 -->
<!-- lem-66: body_md -->
\label{l.rho-BT}
 For each $M$ there is a constant $A=A(M)$ as follows: If $r>0$ and $r\in {\mathsf{BT}}(M)$, then  $\frac{1+r}{1-r}\in {\mathsf{BT}}(A)$.
<!-- end lem-66 -->
<!-- proof-94: body_md -->
Fix $r>0$ in ${\mathsf{BT}}(M)$, $0<c(M)<(M+2)^{-1}(M+1)^{-2},$ and  let  $\rho:=\frac{1+r}{1-r}$.
  


Since $r\in{\mathsf{BT}}(M)$,  for any 
 fraction $\frac{p}{q}$, $$\left|r-\frac{p}{q}\right|> \frac{c(M)}{q^2}$$ (see e.g.  the proof of  \cite[Thm 23]{Khintchine-Continued-Fractions}). In particular
$
|r-1|>c(M).
$ 



Let $\varphi(t):=\frac{1+t}{1-t}$. The inverse function of $\varphi(t)$ is  $\psi(s)=\frac{s-1}{s+1}$. Clearly, $\psi(t)$ is bounded away from $s=-1$.  Therefore, there exists $K=K(M)$ such that 
$$
|\psi(s)|>K\Rightarrow |s+1|<c(M)/2.
$$

\medskip
\noindent
{\em Step 1.\/} There exists a positive constant $c^\#(M)$ which only depends on $M$ as follows. 
Suppose $\frac{p}{q}$ is a          
fraction such that  (a) $|\frac{p}{q}+1|<\frac{M+3}{c(M)}$; (b) $|\psi(\frac{p}{q})|\leq K$; and \\(c) the interval with endpoints $r, \psi(\frac{p}{q})$ does not contain $1$.  
                       
                                         
                                                                              
                                  
                                                                               
                
Then $|\rho-\frac{p}{q}|>c^\#(M)/q^2$. 

\noindent
\medskip
{\em Proof of Step 1.\/} Note that $\psi(p/q)=\frac{p-q}{p+q}$. 
By (c), $\varphi$ is smooth on the interval $I$ with endpoints $r,\psi(p/q)$. By the  mean value theorem,
\begin{align*}
&\left|\rho-\frac{p}{q}\right|=\left|\varphi(r)
-\varphi\left(\frac{p-q}{p+q}\right)\right|\geq \inf_{\xi\in I}{|\varphi'(\xi)|}\left|r-\frac{p-q}{p+q}\right|.
\end{align*}

By our assumptions on $r$,  $0<r<M+1$. By (b), $I\subseteq \{t:|t|<\max\{M+1, K\}\}$. Let 
$
\mu(M):=\inf\{|\varphi'(\xi)|:\; |\xi|\leq \max\{M+1, K\},\; \xi\neq 1\}
$ 
(this is a positive number because $\displaystyle |\varphi'(\xi)|=2/(\xi-1)^2$). 
Thus, by the choice of $c(M)$ and the assumption on $r$,
\begin{align*}
& 
\left|\rho-\frac{p}{q}\right|\geq \mu(M)\cdot \left|r-\frac{p-q}{p+q}\right|
                                                   
\geq \frac{\mu(M)c(M)}{(p+q)^2}=\frac{\mu(M)c(M)}{(1+\frac{p}{q})^2}\cdot \frac{1}{q^2}\geq \frac{\mu(M)c(M)}{c(M)^{-2}(M+3)^2}\cdot \frac{1}{q^2}
\end{align*}
 by (a).
 Now take $c^\#(M):=\mu(M)c(M)^3(M+3)^{-2}$. 


\medskip
\noindent
{\em Step 2.\/} There exists a constant $c^\flat(M)$ which only depends on $M$ as follows.  If a 
         
fraction $p/q$ does not satisfy some of the conditions (a)--(c) above, then $|\rho-\frac{p}{q}|>\frac{c^\flat(M)}{q^2}$. 



\medskip
\noindent
{\em Proof of Step 2.\/} 
If (a) fails, then $|\frac{p}{q}+1|\geq \frac{M+3}{c(M)}$. Since  $|\rho+1|=\frac{2}{|r-1|}<2/c(M)$, we have
$\left|
\rho-\frac{p}{q}\right|\geq \left||\rho+1|-|\tfrac{p}{q}+1|\right|>\frac{M+1}{c(M)}>1\geq \frac{1}{q^2}.
$

If (b) fails, then $|\psi(p/q)|>K$, and by the choice of $K$, $|\frac{p}{q}+1|<c(M)/2$. On the other hand, $|\rho+1|=\frac{2}{|r-1|}>\frac{2}{M+1}>2(M+1)(M+2)c(M)>c(M)$, whence
$\left|
\rho-\frac{p}{q}\right|=|(\rho+1)-(\frac{p}{q}+1)|>c(M)/2>(c(M)/2)/q^2
$.

Finally, if (c) fails and $1$ lies between $r$ and $\psi(p/q)$, then either $0<r<1<\psi(p/q)$ or $0<\psi(p/q)<1<r$ or $\psi(p/q)\leq 0<1<r$. In the first two cases, $\rho=\varphi(r)$ and $p/q=\varphi(\psi(p/q))$ have different signs, whence 
$$
\left|
\rho-\frac{p}{q}
\right|>|\rho|=\frac{1+r}{|1-r|}>\frac{1}{|r-1|}>\frac{1}{c(M)}>1\geq \frac{1}{q^2}.
$$
In the third case, since $\varphi(t)$ is increasing on $(-\infty,1)$ and on $(1,\infty)$, \\ $\rho=\varphi(r)<\varphi(M+1)=-\frac{M+2}{M}$ and $\frac{p}{q}=\varphi(\psi(p/q))>\lim\limits_{s\to-\infty}\varphi(s)=-1$, so 
$$
\left|
\rho-\frac{p}{q}
\right|>\left|1-\frac{M+2}{M}\right|=\frac{2}{M}\geq \frac{2M^{-1}}{q^2}.
$$
Step 2 follows with $c^\flat(M):=\min\{c(M)/2,1,2/M\}=c(M)/2$. 

\medskip
\noindent
{\em Proof of the Lemma.\/} Let $b=b(M):=\min\{c^\sharp(M), c^\flat(M)\}$, then $|\rho-\frac{p}{q}|\geq b/q^2$ for every          
fraction $p/q$. By the theory of continued fractions (see e.g. equation (34) in \cite{Khintchine-Continued-Fractions}), all the partial quotients with positive index of $\rho$ are bounded above by $1/b$. 
The zeroth partial quotient is bounded above by 
$$
|\rho|+1\leq  |\rho+1|+2\leq \frac{2}{|r-1|}+2\leq \frac{2}{c(M)}+2. 
$$
The lemma follows with $A:=\max\{b(M),2c(M)^{-1}+2\}$.
<!-- end proof-94 -->
<!-- lem-67: body_md -->
For every $\varepsilon, M$ there exists $T$ as follows. Suppose $|\rho|\in{\mathsf{BT}}(M)$. Then any line segment in $\mathbb R^2$ with slope $\rho$ and length $L>T$ projects to an  $\varepsilon$-dense curve in $\mathbb T^2:=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$.
<!-- end lem-67 -->
<!-- proof-95: body_md -->
We use the fundamental domain $\mathbb T^2:=[0,1)^2$.  Applying one of the symmetries of $\mathbb T^2$, we may reduce the claim to the case when $0<\rho<1$. Then any line of length $L$ contains at least 
$
n\geq L(1+\rho^2)^{-1/2}-2
$
parallel line segments of length $\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$ and slope $\rho$ extending across $[0,1)^2$ from left to right, and starting at heights
\begin{equation}\label{e.set-of-heights}
\{x_0\}, \{x_0+\rho\},\ldots,\{x_0+n\rho\}.
\end{equation}

Clearly, if these points are $\varepsilon$ dense in $\mathbb T$, then our line is $\varepsilon$-dense in $\mathbb T^2$.
Thus the claim reduces to the following well-known fact in diophantine geometry: For all $\varepsilon,M$ there exists $n=n(\varepsilon,M)$ so that the set \eqref{e.set-of-heights} is $\varepsilon$-dense in $\mathbb T$ whenever all the partial quotients of $\rho$ are less than $M$. (See  \cite[Prop 5.6]{Adiceam-Solomon-Weiss} for a deeper statement.)
<!-- end proof-95 -->
<!-- head-23: body_md -->
Reflecting the fundamental domain $[0,2]\times [0,1]$ across the axis $x=1$ we may assume without loss of generality that $r>0$. 
 Recall that $\mathsf{St}_0$ is isometric to torus $\mathbb R^2/\sqrt{2}\mathbb Z^2$. In this identification, lines with slope $r$ on $\mathsf{St}_0$ are mapped to lines with slope $\rho:=\frac{1+r}{1-r}$ on $\mathbb R^2/\sqrt{2}\mathbb Z^2$ (see Figure \ref{Figure-Staircase} (c)). By Lemma  \ref{l.rho-BT},  $\rho\in{\mathsf{BT}}(A)$ for some constant $A$ which only depends on $M$. Now apply the previous lemma. \hfill$\square$
<!-- end head-23 -->
<!-- head-24: body_md -->
{\em 
Let $\beta\in (-1,1)$ be an irrational with even CFE  $\beta:=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$, and let $L_0$ denote the ray in direction $\beta\choose 1$,  which begins at  the singularity ${\widetilde{\omega}}_0$, in the middle of the top side of rectangle $\mathsf R_0$. Let $\frak{z}_n$ denote the $\mathbb Z$-coordinate of the horizontal rectangle which contains the beginning of  $(\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0)(L_0)$. Then
$$
\frak{z}_n=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{nN_0} \bigl[\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k-1})\bigr].
$$
}
<!-- end head-24 -->
<!-- lem-68: body_md -->
\label{l.bb-id}
$\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0=(H_{-2m_{2nN_0}}\circ V_{-2m_{2nN_0-1}})\circ \cdots\circ (H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})$.
<!-- end lem-68 -->
<!-- proof-96: body_md -->
If $\delta(\widetilde{\psi})$ denotes the drift defined in \eqref{Eq-Drift-Defn}, then $\delta(\widetilde{\psi}_1\circ \widetilde{\psi}_2)=\delta(\widetilde{\psi}_1)+\delta(\widetilde{\psi}_2)$, see \cite{Avila-Dolgopyat-Duryev-Sarig}.  Therefore, on both sides of the equation we have homogeneous automorphisms with zero drift. 
The derivatives  are the same: By \eqref{e.mat-prod-form}, the derivative of  $\widetilde{\psi}_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ\widetilde{\psi}_0$ equals 
$
A_{nN_0}(\beta)
$, and by \eqref{e.A-k}, this is also the derivative of the right-hand-side.
By   Proposition \ref{Prop-Automorphisms}, a homogeneous automorphism with zero drift is  uniquely determined by its derivative. Therefore the two sides of the equation are equal.
<!-- end proof-96 -->
<!-- lem-69: body_md -->
\label{l.composition-formula}
$H_{-2m_{i+1}}\circ V_{-2m_i}$ is given in coordinates by 
$$
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
x \\
y \\
{\mathfrak{z}}
\end{array}
\right)_{\!\!\!H}\!\!\!\!\mapsto
\left(
  \begin{array}{ccc}
    4m_i m_{i+1}+1 & -2m_{i+1} & 0 \\
    -2m_i & 1  & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
x \\
y \\
{\mathfrak{z}}
\end{array}
\right)_{\!\!\!H}+\left(
\begin{array}{c}
Z_i \\
0 \\
-Z_i
\end{array}
\right)
\begin{array}{l}
\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z\\
\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$}\mathbb Z\\
\ \\
\end{array}
$$
<!-- end lem-69 -->
<!-- proof-97: body_md -->
$H^i_{00}({\mathfrak{z}})$ is inside the top half of vertical rectangle ${\mathfrak{z}}-1$, so on $H^i_{00}({\mathfrak{z}})$ we have
\begin{align*}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H&\!\!\!=
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V \xmapsto[]{V_{-2m_i}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    \{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]} \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V\\
&=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x\\
     \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H,\textrm{ because }\{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\in (1,2]\\
&\xmapsto[]{H_{-2m_{i+1}}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     \left\{x-2m_{i+1}\{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\right\}_{(0,2]}\\
     \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H.
\end{align*}
Modulo $2\mathbb Z$, the $x$-coordinate equals to  $(4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x-2m_{i+1} y$. Thus on $H^i_{00}({\mathfrak{z}})$
\begin{equation}\label{e.H00}
(H_{-2m_{i+1}}\circ V_{-2m_i}):
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\mapsto  \left(
  \begin{array}{rll}
    (4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x&-2m_{i+1} y &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z\\
    -2m_i x&+y &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} \mathbb Z \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} &&\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H .
\end{equation}

Similarly, on $H_{01}^i({\mathfrak{z}})$
\begin{align}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x \\
     y\\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H&\!\!\!=
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V \xmapsto[]{V_{-2m_i}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    \{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]} \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V\notag\\
&=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x+1 \\
     \{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}-1\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H,\textrm{ because }\{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\in (0,1]\notag\\
&\xmapsto[]{H_{-2m_{i+1}}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     \left\{x+1-2m_{i+1}\{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\right\}_{(0,2]}\\
     \{y+1-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\notag\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}-1\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H.
\end{align}
Modulo $2\mathbb Z$, the $x$-coordinate equals $(4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x-2m_{i+1}y+1$. Modulo $\mathbb Z$, the $y$-coordinate equals $-2m_i x+y$. Thus,  on $H^i_{01}({\mathfrak{z}})$, 
\begin{equation}\label{e.H01}
(H_{-2m_{i+1}}\circ V_{-2m_i}):
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\!\!\!\mapsto\!  \left(
  \begin{array}{rlll}
    (4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x&-2m_{i+1} y &+1 &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z\\
    -2m_i x &+y & &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} \mathbb Z \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} & &-1&\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H
\end{equation}


$H_{10}^i({\mathfrak{z}})$ is inside the bottom half of vertical rectangle ${\mathfrak{z}}$, so on $H_{10}^i({\mathfrak{z}})$,
\begin{align*}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x \\
     y\\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H&\!\!\!=
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x-1 \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V \xmapsto[]{V_{-2m_i}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x-1 \\
    \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]} \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V\\
&=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
  x\\
  \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\\
  {\mathfrak{z}}\\
    \end{array}
\right)_H,\textrm{ because }\{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\in (0,1] \\
&\xmapsto[]{H_{-2m_{i+1}}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \{x-2m_{i+1}\{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\}_{(0,2]}\\
    \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}\\
    {\mathfrak{z}}\\
  \end{array}
\right)_{H}.
\end{align*}
The $x$-coordinate equals $(4m_i m_{i+1}+1)x-2m_{i+1}y\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z$, and the $y$-coordinate equals $y-2m_i x\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$}\mathbb Z$. So on $H^i_{10}({\mathfrak{z}})$
\begin{equation}\label{e.H10}
(H_{-2m_{i+1}}\circ V_{-2m_i}):
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\mapsto  \left(
  \begin{array}{rll}
    (4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x&-2m_{i+1} y &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z\\
    -2m_i x &+y &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} \mathbb Z \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} & &\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H
\end{equation}



Similarly, on $H_{11}^i({\mathfrak{z}})$ we have
\begin{align*}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x \\
     y\\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H&\!\!\!=
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
     x-1\\
     y\\
     {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_V \xmapsto[]{V_{-2m_i}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x-1 \\
     \{y-2m_i(x-1)\}_{(0,2]}\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}\\
  \end{array}
\right)_V=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x-1 \\
     \{y-2m_ix\}_{(0,2]}\\
     {\mathfrak{z}}\\
  \end{array}
\right)_V\\
&=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
  x-1\\
  \{y-2m_i x\}_{(0,2]}-1\\
  {\mathfrak{z}}+1\\
    \end{array}
\right)_H,\textrm{ because }\{y-2m_ix\}_{(0,2]}\in (1,2]  \\
&\xmapsto[]{H_{-2m_{i+1}}}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
\{x-1-2m_{i+1}\{y-2m_ix\}_{(0,2]}\}_{(0,2]}\\
\{y-2m_ix\}_{(0,2]}-1\\
{\mathfrak{z}}+1\\
  \end{array}
\right)_{H}.
\end{align*}
The $x$-coordinate equals $(4m_i m_{i+1}+1)x-2m_{i+1}y -1\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z$, and the $y$-coordinate equals $y-2m_i x \mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$}\mathbb Z$. So on $H^i_{11}(\xi)$
\begin{equation}\label{e.H11}
(H_{-2m_{i+1}}\circ V_{-2m_i}):
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    x \\
    y \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\!\!\!\!\!\mapsto\!\!  \left(
  \begin{array}{rlll}
    (4m_{i+1}m_i+1)x&-2m_{i+1} y &-1&\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} 2\mathbb Z\\
    -2m_i x &+y & &\mbox{$\,\mathrm{mod}\,$} \mathbb Z \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} & & +1&\\
  \end{array}
\right)_H
\end{equation}

Together, \eqref{e.H00}--\eqref{e.H11} imply the lemma.
<!-- end proof-97 -->
<!-- lem-70: body_md -->
\label{l.sign}
Suppose $n_k\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ for all $k$, and $[0;2n_1,2n_2,\ldots]\not\in\mathbb Q$. Then
$$
2n_1\cdot [0;2n_1,2n_2,\ldots]\textrm{ is in }\begin{cases}
(0,1) & \textrm{when }n_1 n_2>0\\
(1,2) & \textrm{when }n_1 n_2<0.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end lem-70 -->
<!-- proof-98: body_md -->
We saw in Lemma \ref{l.limit-cfe-exists} that 
$
\displaystyle[0;2k_1,2k_2,\ldots]=\lim_{N\to\infty}(v_{2k_1}\circ\cdots\circ v_{2k_N})(0)$,  where $\displaystyle v_{2m}(t)=\frac{1}{2m+t}$. Since $v_{2m}[-1,1]\subset [-1,1]$ for  $m\in 2\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, 
$
[0;2k_1,2k_2,\ldots]\in [-1,1]$. Since $-v_{2m}(t)=v_{-2m}(-t)$, 
$
-[0;2k_1,2k_2,\ldots]=[0;-2k_1,-2k_2,\ldots].
$
We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{e.sign-of-ecfe}
\mathrm{sgn}[0;2n_1,2n_2,\ldots]=\mathrm{sgn}(n_1).
\end{equation}
Indeed, $[0;2n_1,2n_2,\ldots]=\mathrm{sgn}(n_1)\cdot [0;|2n_1|,\pm 2n_2,\pm 2n_3,\ldots]\in\{\frac{\mathrm{sgn}(n_1)}{|2n_1|+t}: t\in [-1,1]\}$, and the denominator is always positive.



Let $s_i:=\mathrm{sgn}(n_i)$, then
\begin{align*}
&2n_1\cdot [0;2n_1,2n_2,\ldots]=|2n_1|\cdot [0;|2n_1|,2n_2s_1,2n_3s_1,2n_4s_1,\ldots]\\
&=|2n_1|\cdot [0;|2n_1|,|2n_2|s_1 s_2,2n_3s_1,2n_4s_1,\ldots]=\frac{|2n_1|}{|2n_1|+[0;|2n_2|s_1 s_2,2n_3 s_1,\ldots]}
\end{align*}
By \eqref{e.sign-of-ecfe}, the even CFE in the denominator is in $[0,1]$ when  $s_1 s_2=1$, and in $[-1,0]$,  when $s_1 s_2=-1$. In the first case the fraction is in $(0,1]$. In the second case it is inside
$
\{\frac{|2n_1|}{|2n_1|-t}: t\in [0,1]\}\subset [1,2]
$. The possibilities $0,1,2$ are ruled out by irrationality.
<!-- end proof-98 -->
<!-- lem-71: body_md -->
\label{l.twist-positive-1}
Suppose $\beta_1=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$ is irrational, and $o$ is the singularity at the bottom left side of horizontal rectangle ${\mathfrak{z}}$, and ${\widehat o}$ the singularity at the middle top side of horizontal rectangle ${\mathfrak{z}}\pm 1$ (${\widehat o}$ is congruent to $o$).
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $m_1 m_2>0$, then
$\displaystyle
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})\right]=L\left(o, {E^2(\beta_1)\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}}\right).
$
\item If $m_1 m_2<0$, then
$\displaystyle
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})\right]=
L\left({\widehat o}, -{E^2(\beta_1)\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}}-\operatorname{sgn}(m_1)\right).
$
\end{enumerate}
Here $E$ is the even Gauss map, i.e. $E^2(\beta_1)=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]$.
<!-- end lem-71 -->
<!-- proof-99: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\item If $m_1>0$, then $\beta_1>0$, and $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$ begins with the segment
$\left(
   \begin{array}{c}
     t\beta_1 \\
     t \\
     {\mathfrak{z}} \\
   \end{array}
 \right)_H
 $,  $0<t\ll 1$. In particular, the ray starts at $ H_{00}^1\cup H_{01}^1$. To see which of these possibilities happens, we use Lemma \ref{l.sign} to see that  for small positive $t$,
 $$
 \{y-2m_1 x\}_{(0,2]}=\{t(1-2m_1[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots])\}_{(0,2]}\in \begin{cases}
 (0,1) & m_1 m_2>0\\
 (1,2) & m_1 m_2<0.
 \end{cases}
 $$
Thus, if $m_1>0$ and $m_1m_2>0$ then $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},0)$ starts at $H_{00}^1$, and if $m_1>0$ and $m_1 m_2<0$, then $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},0)$ starts at $H_{01}^1$.


\item
If $m_1<0$, then $\beta_1<0$, and
 $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$ begins with
$\left(
   \begin{array}{c}
     2+t\beta_1 \\
     t \\
     {\mathfrak{z}} \\
   \end{array}
 \right)_H\!\!\! ,0<t\ll 1$, so the ray starts at $H_{10}^i$ or $H_{11}^i$. By Lemma \ref{l.sign}:
  \begin{align*}
\{y-2m_1 x\}_{(0,2]}=\{t-2m_1(2+t\beta_1)\}_{(0,2]}=\{t(1-2m_1\beta_1)\}_{(0,2]}\in
\begin{cases}
(0,1) & m_1 m_2>0\\
(1,2) & m_1 m_2<0.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
Thus, if $m_1<0$ and $m_1 m_2>0$ then $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$ starts at $H_{10}^1$, and if $m_1<0$ and  $m_1 m_2<0$, then 
$L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$ starts at $H_{11}^1$.
 \end{enumerate}

We now apply $H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1}$ to $L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$. By Lemma \ref{l.composition-formula}, the result is a linear ray which begins with the segment
\begin{align*}
&\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \!\!\!\left\{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1 t -2m_2t+Z_1\right\}_{(0,2]}\!\!\! \\
    \left\{-2m_1 \beta_1 t+t\right\}_{(0,1]} \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-Z_1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H (0<t\ll 1),
\textrm{ where }
    
Z_1\!\!=\!\!\begin{cases}
+1 & m_1\!\!>\!\!0, \, m_1 m_2\!\!<\!\!0\\
-1 & m_1\!\!<\!\!0,\, m_1 m_2\!\!<\!\!0\\
0& \textrm{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
Equivalently,  $Z_1=\mathrm{sgn}(m_1)\times \frac{1-\mathrm{sgn}(m_1 m_2)}{2}.$

Let us simplify the horizontal coordinates.

Suppose first that $m_1 m_2>0$. Then $Z_1=0$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (0,1)$. Therefore for all $t$ small, $-2m_1\beta_1 t+t\in (0,1)$. Changing coordinates $\tau=-2m_1\beta_1t+t$, and noting that $\tau>0$,  we see that our ray starts
with
$$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \left\{\tau \left(\frac{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1  -2m_2}{-2m_1 \beta_1 +1}\right)\right\}_{(0,2]} \\
    \tau \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<\tau\ll 1).
$$
Next, ${\tiny
\left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
    4m_1 m_2+1 & -2m_2 \\
    -2m_1 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)=
\left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
    1 & -2m_2 \\
    0 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)
\left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
    1 & 0 \\
    -2m_1 & 1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)}
$, therefore
$$
\frac{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1  -2m_2}{-2m_1 \beta_1 +1}=-2m_2+\cfrac{1}{-2m_1+\cfrac{1}{\beta_1}}=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]=E^2(\beta).
$$
This is positive when $m_3>0$ and negative when $m_3<0$. So our ray starts with
$$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \tau E^2(\beta)+(1-\operatorname{sgn}(m_3)) \\
    \tau \\
    {\mathfrak{z}} \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<\tau\ll 1).
$$
Either way, if $m_1 m_2>0$, then 
$(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})[L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})]
=L(o,{\beta_2\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})$, where $$\beta_2:=E^2(\beta_1)=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots].$$

Next suppose $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1>0$. In this case $Z_1=+1$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (1,2)$. Therefore for all $t>0$ small, we have the following identities for the $x$ and $y$ coordinates:
$$
\{(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1t-2m_2 t+Z_1\}_{(0,2]}=
(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1t-2m_2 t+1,
$$
$$
\{-2m_1\beta_1 t+t\}_{(0,1]}=t(1-2m_1\beta_1)+1.
$$
It follows that our ray begins with
\begin{align*}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    (4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1t-2m_2 t+1 \\
    t(1-2m_1\beta_1)+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<t\ll 1)
\end{align*}
Changing coordinates into $\tau:=-t(1-2m_1\beta_1)$ (we need the minus to keep $\tau$ positive), we can rewrite this as
\begin{align*}
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    -\tau\left(\frac{(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1-2m_2}{-2m_1\beta_1+1}\right) +1 \\
    -\tau+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<\tau\ll 1)
\end{align*}
(Note that  as  $\tau\!\!\to \!\!0^{+}$,  we obtain the  singularity $\widehat{o}
=(1,1,{\mathfrak{z}}-1)_H$, which is congruent to $o=(0,0,{\mathfrak{z}})_H$.)
The $x$-coordinate simplifies as before to $-\tau\beta_2+1$, where $\beta_2=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]$. In summary, if $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1>0$, then
$$
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})[L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})]
=L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_2\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}}-1)\textrm{,  } \beta_2:=E^2(\beta_1)=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots].
$$

Finally, suppose $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1<0$. In this case, $Z_1=-1$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (1,2)$. Therefore, for all $t>0$ small, the $x$ and $y$ coordinates are given for $t>0$ small by
$$
\left\{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1 t -2m_2t-1\right\}_{(0,2]}=(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1 t -2m_2t+1
$$
$$
 \left\{-2m_1 \beta_1 t+t\right\}_{(0,1]}=t(1-2m_1\beta)+1
$$
So our ray begins with
$$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    (4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1 t -2m_2t+1 \\
     t(1-2m_1\beta)+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}+1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H \ (0<t\ll 1).
$$
As before, we can rewrite this in the form
$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    -\tau\beta_2+1 \\
     -\tau+1 \\
    {\mathfrak{z}}+1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H \ (0<\tau\ll 1),
$
whence $(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})[L(o,{\beta_1\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}})]=
L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_2\choose 1},{\mathfrak{z}}+1)$.

Looking at all these cases, we obtain the lemma.
<!-- end proof-99 -->
<!-- lem-72: body_md -->
\label{l.twist-negative}
Suppose $\beta_1=[0;2m_1,2m_2,\ldots]$ is irrational, and ${\widehat o}$ is the singularity at the middle top  side of horizontal rectangle $\eta$. Let $o$ be the singularity at the bottom left corner of horizontal rectangle $\eta\pm 1$ (which is congruent to ${\widehat o}$).
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $m_1 m_2>0$, then
$$
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L\left({\widehat o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta\right)\right]=
L\left( {\widehat o},-{\beta_2\choose 1},\eta\right),\textrm{ where }\beta_2=E^2(\beta).
$$
\item If $m_1 m_2<0$, then
$$
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L\left({\widehat o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta\right)\right]=L\left(o,{\beta_2\choose 1},\eta-\operatorname{sgn}(m_1)\right),
$$
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-72 -->
<!-- proof-100: body_md -->
$\bullet$ If $m_1>0$, then $\beta_1>0$, and $L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta)$ begins with the segment
$\left(
   \begin{array}{c}
     1-t\beta_1 \\
     1-t \\
     \eta \\
   \end{array}
 \right)_{\!\!\!H}
 $, $0\!\!<\!\!t\!\ll\! 1$. In particular, the ray starts at $H_{00}^1\!\cup\! H_{01}^1$. By  Lemma \ref{l.sign} for small positive $t$
 $$
 \{y-2m_1 x\}_{(0,2]}=\{1-t-2m_1+2m_1\beta_1t\}_{(0,2]}\in \begin{cases}
 (0,1) & m_1 m_2>0\\
  (1,2) & m_1 m_2<0.
 \end{cases}
 $$
 So if $m_1>0$ and $m_1m_2>0$ then $L(\widehat{o},{ -{\beta_1\choose 1}},0)$ starts at $H_{00}^1$, and if $m_1>0$ and $m_1 m_2<0$, then $L(\widehat{o},{- {\beta_1\choose 1}},\xi)$ starts at $H_{01}^1$.


$\bullet$
If $m_1<0$, then $\beta_1<0$, and
 $L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta)$ begins with
$\left(
   \begin{array}{c}
     1-t\beta_1 \\
     1-t \\
     \eta \\
   \end{array}
 \right)_{\!\!\!H},$ $0<t\ll 1$, so the ray starts at $H_{10}^1$ or $H_{11}^1$. As before, by  Lemma \ref{l.sign},
  \begin{align*}
\{y-2m_1 x\}_{(0,2]}=\{1-t-2m_1+2m_1\beta_1 t\}_{(0,2]}\in
\begin{cases}
(0,1) & m_1 m_2>0\\
(1,2) & m_1 m_2<0.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
So if $m_1<0$ and $m_1 m_2>0$ then $L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta)$ starts at $H_{10}^i$, and if $m_1<0$ and  $m_1 m_2<0$, then $L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta)$ starts at $H_{11}^i$.
 

By Lemma \ref{l.composition-formula},  $(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})
[L(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta)]$ begins with the segment
\begin{align*}
&\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \left\{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) (1-\beta_1 t) -2m_2(1-t)+Z_1\right\}_{(0,2]} \\
    \left\{-2m_1 (1-\beta_1  t)+(1-t)\right\}_{(0,1]} \\
    \eta-Z_1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<t\ll 1),
\textrm{ where }\\
&Z_1=\begin{cases}
+1 & m_1>0, m_1 m_2<0\\
-1 & m_1<0, m_1 m_2<0\\
0& \textrm{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
$Z_1$ is exactly the same as we had before. But the horizontal coordinates are now
\begin{align*}
&\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \left\{-(4m_1 m_{2}+1)\beta_1 t +2m_2t+Z_1+1\right\}_{(0,2]} \\
    \left\{2m_1 \beta_1t-t\right\}_{(0,1]} \\
    \eta-Z_1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<t\ll 1),
\end{align*}


Suppose first that $m_1 m_2>0$. Then $Z_1=0$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (0,1)$. Therefore for all $t>0$ small, $2m_1\beta_1 t-t<0$ and $\{2m_1\beta_1 t-t\}_{(0,1]}=1+2m_1\beta_1 t-t$. Changing coordinates $\tau=-2m_1\beta_1t+t$, we see that our ray starts with
$$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \{-\tau \left(\frac{(4m_1 m_{2}+1) \beta_1  -2m_2}{-2m_1 \beta_1 +1}\right)+1\}_{(0,2]} \\
    \{1-\tau\}_{(0,1]} \\
    \eta \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H
=\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    1-\tau \beta_2 \\
    1-\tau \\
    \eta \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H
\ \ (0<\tau\ll 1).
$$
Here, as before, $\beta_2=[0;2m_3,2m_4,\ldots]=E^2(\beta_1)$.
In summary, if $m_1 m_2>0$, then $$(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L\left(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta\right)\right]
=L\left(\widehat{o},-{\beta_2\choose 1},\eta\right).$$

Next suppose $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1>0$. In this case $Z_1=+1$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (1,2)$. For $t>0$ small, the $y$-coordinate  equals
$\displaystyle
\{2m_1\beta t-t\}_{(0,1]}=(2m_1\beta-1) t=:\tau>0.
$
This allows us to simplify the $x$-coordinate into
\begin{align*}
&\{-(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1 t+2m_2t\}_{(0,2]}=\left\{\tau\cdot \frac{-(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1 +2m_2}{2m_1\beta-1} \right\}_{(0,2]}\\
&=
\left\{\tau\cdot \frac{(4m_1 m_2+1)\beta_1 -2m_2}{-2m_1\beta_1+1} \right\}_{(0,2]}=\left\{\tau\left(-2m_2+\cfrac{1}{-2m_1+\cfrac{1}{\beta_1}}\right) \right\}_{(0,2]}\\
&=\{\tau \beta_2\}_{(0,2]},\textrm{ where }\beta_2=[0;2m_3,2m_3,\ldots]=E^2(\beta_1)\\
&=(1-\mathrm{sgn}(m_3))-\tau\beta_2\textrm{ (because $m_3<0\Leftrightarrow \tau\beta_2<0$ and then we must add $2$).}
\end{align*}
It follows that our ray begins with
$\displaystyle
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \tau\beta_2+(1-\mathrm{sgn}(m_3)) \\
    \tau \\
    \eta-1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H\ \ (0<\tau\ll 1).
$
So if $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1>0$, then
$$
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L\left(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta\right)\right]=L\left(o,{\beta_2\choose 1},\eta-1\right), \textrm{ where }\beta_2:=E^2(\beta_1).
$$

Finally, suppose $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1<0$. In this case, $Z_1=-1$ and $2m_1\beta_1\in (1,2)$. Therefore,  the $y$ and $x$ coordinates are given for $t>0$ small by
$$
 \left\{2m_1 \beta_1t-t\right\}_{(0,1]}=(2m_1\beta_1-1)t=:\tau>0
$$
\begin{align*}
&\left\{-(4m_1 m_{2}+1)\beta_1 t +2m_2t\right\}_{(0,2]}=\{\tau\left(\tfrac{-(4m_1 m_1+1)\beta_1+2m_2}{2m_1\beta_1-1}\right)\}_{(0,2]}\\
                                                                                
                                                                                     
&=\{\tau\beta_2\}_{(0,2]},\textrm{ where }\beta_2=E^2(\beta)=[0;2m_3,2m_3,\ldots]\\
&=(1-\mathrm{sgn}(m_3))+\tau\beta_2.
\end{align*}
So our ray begins with
$
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \tau\beta_2+ (1-\mathrm{sgn}(m_3))\\
     \tau \\
    \eta+1 \\
  \end{array}
\right)_H \ (0<\tau\ll 1).
$
In summary,  if $m_1 m_2<0$ and $m_1<0$, then
$
(H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\left[L\left(\widehat{o},-{\beta_1\choose 1},\eta\right)\right]=
L\left(o,{\beta_2\choose 1},\eta+1\right).
$

The lemma follows.
<!-- end proof-100 -->
<!-- head-25: body_md -->
By Lemma \ref{l.bb-id}, to prove the theorem we need to find the  $\mathbb Z$-coordinate of the horizontal rectangle which contains the beginning of
\begin{align*}
L_n&=\left(H_{-2m_{2nN_0}}\circ V_{-2m_{2nN_0-1}})\circ \cdots\circ (H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\right)\left[L\left(\widehat{o},{\beta\choose 1},(-1)\right)\right]
\end{align*}
(the minus one is needed  because $\widehat{o}$ is on the top side of the horizontal rectangle, and we want the initial ray to start at rectangle zero). Since  the  midpoint of the top side of horizontal rectangle (-1) is the bottom left corner of horizontal rectangle zero,  
\begin{align*}
L_n&=\left(H_{-2m_{2nN_0}}\circ V_{-2m_{2nN_0-1}})\circ \cdots\circ (H_{-2m_2}\circ V_{-2m_1})\right)\left[L\left({o},{\beta\choose 1},0\right)\right]
\end{align*}

$L_n$ is given recursively  by $L_0=L\left({o},{\beta\choose 1},0\right)$ and $L_{k+1}=(H_{-2m_{2k+2}}\circ V_{-2m_{2k+1}})(L_k)$. 
An inductive argument using Lemmas \ref{l.twist-positive-1} and \ref{l.twist-negative} shows that either   $L_k=L(o,{E^{2k}(\beta)\choose 1},\cdot)$ (``case A") or $L_k=L(\widehat{o},-{E^{2k}(\beta)\choose 1},\cdot)$ (``case B"). Let $\Delta_{k+1}$ denote the horizontal $\mathbb Z$ coordinate of the beginning of $L_{k+1}$ minus  that of $L_k$. $\Delta_{k+1}$ is determined by   Lemma~\ref{l.twist-positive-1} in case A, and by  Lemma~\ref{l.twist-negative} in case B. In both cases we have
\begin{align*}
\Delta_{k+1}&=\begin{cases}
0 & m_{2k+1}m_{2k+2}>0,\\
-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+1}) & m_{2k+1}m_{2k+2}<0.
\end{cases}\\
&=-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+1})\times \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+1})\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+2}))=
\frac{1}{2} \left[ \operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+2})-\operatorname{sgn}(m_{2k+1})\right].
\end{align*}
 Summing $\Delta_{k+1}$ over $k=0,\ldots,nN_0-1$, we obtain the theorem.
 \hfill$\square$
<!-- end head-25 -->
<!-- defi-11: body_md -->
A Markov array $\mathsf X$ is called  {\em uniformly elliptic},\index{Uniform ellipticity} if there is a  constant $\varepsilon_0$, called an {\em ellipticity constant}, and a representation $\pi_{n,n+1}^{(N)}(y,y')=p_n^{(N)}(y,y')\mu_{n+1}^{(N)}(y')$, where for all $N$ and $0\leq n\leq k_N$, 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\mu_n^{(N)}$ are probability measures on $\mathfrak S_n$;
\item $0\leq p_n^{(N)}(\cdot,\cdot)\leq 1/\varepsilon_0$;
\item $\displaystyle \sum_{y\in\mathfrak S_{n+1}} p_n^{(N)}(x,y)p_{n+1}^{(N)}(y,z)>\varepsilon_0$ for all $x\in\mathfrak S_n^{(N)}, z\in\mathfrak S_{n+2}^{(N)}$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end defi-11 -->
<!-- prop-15: body_md -->
\label{p.mixing-for-arrays}
Let $\mathsf X$ be a uniformly elliptic Markov array with row lengths $k_N+1$. There exist $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $C_{mix}>1$, which only depend on the ellipticity constant, such that
for any functions 
$g_m^{(N)}:\mathfrak{S}_m^{(N)}\to\mathbb{R}, g_n^{(N)}:\mathfrak{S}_n^{(N)}\to\mathbb{R}$ and  $0\leq m<n<k_N+1$,  
\begin{align}
& \left\|{\mathbb{E}}(g_n^{(N)}(X_n^{(N)})|X_m^{(n)})-\mathbb E(g_n^{(N)})\right\|_{L^\infty}<C_{mix} \theta^{n-m} \|g_n^{(N)}\|_{L^\infty}\label{EM-1}\\ 
& \left|{\rm Cov}(g_m^{(N)}(X_m), g_n^{(N)}(X_n))\right|<C_{mix} \theta^{n-m}\sqrt{{\rm Var}(g_m^{(N)}(X^{(n)}_m)){\rm Var}(g_n^{(N)}(X^{(N)}_n))} 
\label{EM-2} 
\end{align}
<!-- end prop-15 -->
<!-- thm-30: body_md -->
\label{LmVarCycles}
Let $\mathsf X$ be a uniformly\index{Variance of $S_N$!in terms of structure constants} elliptic Markov array, and let $\mathsf f$ be a uniformly bounded additive functional on $\mathsf X$. Then there are constants $C_1, C_2$ 
which depend only $\displaystyle \sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty$ and the ellipticity constant,  such that
$$ \frac{U_N}{C_1}-C_2\leq V_N \leq C_1 U_N+C_2. $$
In particular $V_N\to\infty$ iff $U_N\to\infty$, and if $\xi\neq 0$, then  
$V_N\geq C_1^{-1}\xi^{-2}D_N(\xi)-C_2.$
<!-- end thm-30 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\normalfont
In particular, if $\mathsf X$ is a uniformly elliptic Markov \underline{chain}, and $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on $\mathsf X$, then either $V_N\to\infty$ or $V_N$ is bounded. The reason is that in this case $u_n^{(N)}=u_n$, and therefore $U_N\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\sum u_n^2$, which is either finite or infinite. The remark is false for arrays, for obvious reasons.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- defi-12: body_md -->
An additive functional $\mathsf f$ on a Markov array $\mathsf X$ is called {\em center-tight}, if there are constants $m_N\in\mathbb R$ such that for all ${\varepsilon}>0$, there is some $M>0$ such that 
$$
{\mathbb{P}}[|S_N-m_N|>M]<{\varepsilon}\textrm{ for all }N. 
$$
<!-- end defi-12 -->
<!-- thm-31: body_md -->
\label{t.V-n-bounded}
Let $\mathsf X$ be a uniformly elliptic Markov array, and let $\mathsf f$ be a uniformly bounded additive functional on $\mathsf X$. Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $V_N$ is bounded;
\item $\mathsf f$ is center-tight;
\item There exist uniformly bounded additive functionals $\mathsf a$ and $\mathsf h$ on $\mathsf X$ such that \\
$a_n^{(N)}=a_n^{(N)}(X_n^{(N)})$, $h_n^{(N)}=h_n^{(N)}(X_n^{(N)},X_{n+1}^{(N)})$, $\displaystyle\sup_N\sum_{n=1}^{k_N} {\rm Var} [h_n^{(N)}(X_n^{(N)},X_{n+1}^{(N)})]<\infty$, and
\begin{equation}\label{e.coboundary}
f_n^{(N)}=a_{n+1}^{(N)}-a_n^{(N)}+h^{(N)}\textrm{ a.s.}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
In the special case of Markov chains, (3) holds with $a_n^{(N)},h_n^{(N)}$ independent of $N$, and 
$\displaystyle \sum_{n\geq 1} \left[ h_n-\mathbb E(h_n)\right]$ converges a.s.
<!-- end thm-31 -->
<!-- thm-32: body_md -->
\label{ThMCCLT}
Suppose $\mathsf X$ is a uniformly elliptic Markov array, with a uniformly bounded additive functional $\mathsf f$. If $V_N\to\infty$, then for all $a<b$, 
$$
{\mathbb{P}}\left[\frac{S_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N}}\in (a,b)\right]
\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_a^b e^{-t^2/2} dt.
$$
<!-- end thm-32 -->
<!-- thm-33: body_md -->
\label{ThASIP}
Suppose $\mathsf X$ is a uniformly elliptic Markov \underline{chain}, and $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on $\mathsf X$, such that $V_N\to\infty$. Then there exist $\delta>0$,\index{Almost sure invariance principle}
a probability space $(\widetilde\Omega, \widetilde{\mathbb{P}})$ and  measurable functions
${\widetilde S}_N,W(t):{\widetilde{\Omega}}\to\mathbb{R}$ $(N\in \mathbb{N}, t\in \mathbb{R}^+)$ 
so that
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  the stochastic processes $S_N-\mathbb E(S_N)$ and ${\widetilde S}_N$ are equal in distribution;

\item  $W(t)$ is equal in distribution to the  standard Brownian motion;

\item  For a.e. $\omega\in{\widetilde{\Omega}}$, for all $N$ large enough, $|{\widetilde S}_N-W(V_N)|\leq V_N^{1/2-\delta}$. 
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-33 -->
<!-- thm-34: body_md -->
\label{t.LIL}
Suppose $\mathsf X$ is a uniformly elliptic Markov \underline{chain}, and $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on $\mathsf X$, such that $V_N\to\infty$. Then the following holds with probability one:\index{Law of the iterated logarithm}
\begin{equation}
\label{LIL}
\limsup_{N\to\infty} \frac{S_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N\log \log V_N}}=\sqrt{2},
\quad
\liminf_{N\to\infty} \frac{S_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N\log \log V_N}}=-\sqrt{2}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-34 -->
<!-- defi-13: body_md -->
\label{d.alg-rng}
The {\em algebraic range}\index{Algebraic range} of $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is the intersection $G_{alg}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ of all closed subgroups $G$ of $(\mathbb R,+)$ for which there are constants $c^{(N)}_n$ such that 
\begin{equation}\label{e.alg-range}
{\mathbb{P}}[f_n^{(N)}(X_n^{(N)},X_{n+1}^{(N)})-c^{(N)}_n\in G]=1\textrm{ for all }0\leq n\leq k_N, N\in\mathbb N.
\end{equation}
<!-- end defi-13 -->
<!-- defi-14: body_md -->
\label{d.ess-rng}
The {\em essential range}\index{Essential range} of $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is the intersection 
$$
G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f):=\bigcap \left\{G_{alg}(\mathsf X, \mathsf g):\mathsf g-\mathsf f\textrm{ is center-tight} \right\}. 
$$
<!-- end defi-14 -->
<!-- defi-15: body_md -->
An additive functional $\mathsf f$ such that $G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=G_{alg}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$, is called {\em irreducible}\index{Irreducibility} (on $\mathsf X$).
<!-- end defi-15 -->
<!-- defi-16: body_md -->
The {\em co-range} of $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is \index{Co-range}
$
\displaystyle H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f):=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R: 
\sup_N D_N(\xi)<\infty 
\right\}
$
<!-- end defi-16 -->
<!-- thm-35: body_md -->
\label{t.co-range}
Let  $\mathsf X$ be a uniformly elliptic Markov array, with a uniformly bounded additive functional $\mathsf f$. Then  $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is a closed subgroup of $(\mathbb R,+)$, and:\index{Essential range!and the co-range}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\{0\}$, then $G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\mathbb R$;
\item If $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\mathbb R$, then $G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\{0\}$, and $\mathsf f$ is center-tight;
\item If $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=t\mathbb Z$ with $t\neq 0$, then $G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\frac{2\pi}{t}\mathbb Z$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-35 -->
<!-- cor-16: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathsf X$ is uniformly elliptic and $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded  \underline{$\mathbb Z$-valued} additive functional. Then $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is irreducible with essential range $\mathbb Z$, iff for each integer  $\ell>1$, \index{Irreducibility}
$\displaystyle \sup_N D_N(2\pi/\ell)=\infty$ (or for Markov chains, equivalently,  
$\displaystyle \sum d_n^2\left(\frac{2\pi}{\ell}\right)=\infty$).
<!-- end cor-16 -->
<!-- proof-101: body_md -->
Since $\mathsf f$ is integer valued,  $d_n^{(N)}(2\pi k)=0$ for all $k\in\mathbb Z$, and  $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\supset 2\pi\mathbb Z$. Necessarily, $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\mathbb R$, or $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\frac{2\pi}{\ell}\mathbb Z$ for some $\ell\in\mathbb N$. 

Suppose $\displaystyle (\forall\ell\in\mathbb N\setminus\{1\},\ \sup_N D_N(2\pi/\ell)=\infty)$, then  $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\neq \mathbb R$,  and $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\neq \frac{2\pi}{\ell}\mathbb Z$ with $\ell\in\mathbb N\setminus\{1\}$. Thus $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=2\pi\mathbb Z$, and $G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=\mathbb Z$. So
$$\mathbb Z=G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\subset G_{alg}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\subset\mathbb Z,
$$
and $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is irreducible with range $\mathbb Z$. 

Conversely, if 
$G_{ess}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\!\!=\!\!G_{alg}(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\!\!=\!\!\mathbb Z$, then 
$H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\!\!=\!\!2\pi\mathbb Z$, whence 
$\displaystyle \sup_N D_N\left(\frac{2\pi}{\ell}\right)\!\!=\!\!\infty$ for all $\ell\in\mathbb N\setminus\{1\}$.
<!-- end proof-101 -->
<!-- lem-73: body_md -->
\label{LmChange}
Let $\mathsf f$ be a uniformly bounded additive functional on a Markov chain $\mathsf X$. Suppose $\xi_n$ is a bounded sequence of real numbers, and let $\widetilde{\mathsf X}$ denote the Markov arrays with rows $(\widetilde{X}^{\xi_n}_0,\ldots,\widetilde{X}_{n+1}^{\xi_n})$ $(n\geq 1)$, see Section \ref{ss.change-of-measure}. Then \index{Change of measure!structure constants}\index{Change of measure!essential range and irreducibility} \index{Change of measure!hereditary property}\index{Irreducibility!preserved under change of measure}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item The structure constants of $(\widetilde{\mathsf X},\mathsf f)$ are equal up to bounded multiplicative error to the  structure constants of   $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$. 
\item $(\widetilde{\mathsf X},\mathsf f)$ and $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ have the same essential ranges.
\item $\mathsf f$ is irreducible on $\widetilde{\mathsf X}$ iff $\mathsf f$ is irreducible on ${\mathsf X}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-73 -->
<!-- defi-17: body_md -->
\label{d.hereditary}
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is an additive functional on a Markov array $\mathsf X$. We say that $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is {\em hereditary}, if $G_{ess}(\mathsf X', \mathsf f|_{\mathsf X'})=G_{ess}(\mathsf X, \mathsf f)$ for all sub-arrays $\mathsf X'$ of $\mathsf X$.
<!-- end defi-17 -->
<!-- lem-74: body_md -->
\label{l.hereditary}
Suppose $\{X_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ is a uniformly elliptic Markov \underline{chain}, and $\{f_n\}_{n\geq 1}$ is a uniformly bounded  additive functional on $\{X_n\}_{n\geq 1}$. Let  $f^{(N)}_n:=f_n$. 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item Suppose $N_k\uparrow\infty$. The  Markov array with rows $(X_1,\ldots,X_{N_k+1})$,  is  hereditary.
\item  The Markov array with rows $(\widetilde{X}^{\xi_N}_1,\ldots,\widetilde{X
}_{N+1}^{\xi_N})$ obtained from the change of measure in \S\ref{ss.change-of-measure} is hereditary, whenever $\xi_N$ is bounded.
\item Suppose $f_n$ are integer-valued, and for every  $\eta\in \mathbb R\setminus 2\pi\mathbb Z$, 
there are constants $c, M>0$ with the following property:
$$
\forall n\in\mathbb N\, \exists k\in (n,n+M)\cap\mathbb N\textrm{ s.t. } d_k(\eta)>c.
$$
Suppose  $\xi_N\in\mathbb R$ are bounded, $n_N\in\mathbb N$, and  $L_N:=n_{N+1}-n_N\to\infty$. Then the array with rows $(\widetilde{X}^{\xi_N}_{n_N+1},\widetilde{X}_{n_N+2}^{\xi_N},\ldots,\widetilde{X}_{n_{N}+L_N}^{\xi_N})$ is hereditary.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lem-74 -->
<!-- proof-102: body_md -->
We prove part (3). 
Parts (1) and (2) have similar proofs (see  \cite[\S 4.2.3]{Dolgopyat-Sarig-Book} for details). Let   $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ denote  the co-range of our array. To prove the hereditary property, it is sufficient to show that 
$
D_N(\eta)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\infty\textrm{ on $\mathbb R\setminus H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$}
$, because this implies that $H(\mathsf X', \mathsf f|_{\mathsf X'})=H(\mathsf X, \mathsf f)$, whence 
$G_{ess}(\mathsf X', \mathsf f|_{\mathsf X'})=G_{ess}(\mathsf X, \mathsf f)$,
 for every sub-array $\mathsf X'$. 

We denote the structure constants of $\{X_n\}$ by $d_n(\eta)$, and the structure constants of the array in (3) by $d^{(N)}_n(\eta)$. 
By Lemma \ref{LmChange} and the boundedness of $\xi_N$,  $d_j^{(N)}(\eta)\!\!\asymp \!\! d_{n_N+j}(\eta)$. By  assumption, if $\eta\in\mathbb R\setminus 2\pi\mathbb Z$, then 
$
\displaystyle \sum_{j=n_N+3}^{n_N+L_N-3}\!\!\!\!\! d_j(\eta)^2\!\!\gtrsim \!\! c^2 L_N/M
$, and therefore 
 $\displaystyle D_N(\eta)=\sum_{j=3}^{L_N} d_j^{(N)}(\eta)^2\xrightarrow[i\to\infty]{}\infty$ on $\mathbb R\setminus 2\pi\mathbb Z$. 
 In particular, $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\subset 2\pi\mathbb Z$. 
 
 At the same time $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)\supset 2\pi\mathbb Z$, because $\mathsf f$ is integer-valued. So  
 $H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)=2\pi\mathbb Z$ and $D_N(\eta) \xrightarrow[i\to\infty]{}\infty$ on $\mathbb R\setminus H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$.
<!-- end proof-102 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\normalfont
The local limit theorem for irreducible {\em real-valued} additive functionals requires the stronger {\em stable hereditary property}: $D_N(\eta)\to\infty$ {\em uniformly} on compacts in $\mathbb R\setminus H(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$. But for $\mathbb Z$-valued functions, such as those used in this work,  the stable hereditary property and the hereditary property are equivalent \cite[Thm 4.14]{Dolgopyat-Sarig-Book}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- thm-36: body_md -->
\label{t.ThLLT}
Let $\mathsf f$ be an integer-valued,  uniformly bounded, irreducible, and hereditary additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov array $\mathsf X$, with algebraic range $\mathbb Z$. Then $V_N\to\infty$, and for every sequence of   $z_N\in\mathbb Z$ such that $\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N}}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}s$,
$$  
{\mathbb{P}}[S_N=z_N]=[1+o(1)]\frac{e^{-s^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi V_N}},\textrm{ as $N\to\infty$}. 
$$
<!-- end thm-36 -->
<!-- thm-37: body_md -->
\label{ThLLTArrays}
Under the assumptions of  Theorem \ref{t.ThLLT}, if
 $x_1^{(N)}\in\mathfrak S^{(N)}_1$,  $x_{k_N+1}^{(N)}\!\!\in\!\!\mathfrak S^{(N)}_{k_N+1}$, and ${\mathbb{P}}[X^{(N)}_{k_N+1}=x_{k_N+1}^{(N)}]$ is bounded away from zero, then
$$  
{\mathbb{P}}\biggl[S_N=z_N\big|X^{(N)}_{1}=x_{1}^{(N)}\ , \  X^{(N)}_{k_N+1}=x_{k_N+1}^{(N)}\biggr]=[1+o(1)]\frac{e^{-s^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi V_N}},\textrm{ as $N\to\infty$}. 
$$
<!-- end thm-37 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\normalfont
The local limit theorem in the inhomogeneous case was first worked out 
 for sums of bounded  {\em independent} (non-identically distributed) integer-valued random variables, by Prohorov
\cite{Prohorov}. Rozanov extended this work in \cite{Rozanov} to the  unbounded independent case, subject to appropriate tightness conditions. 
The  non-integer  independent case was done first in
in \cite{Dolgopyat-LLT-2016}.

The local limit theorem for homogeneous Markov chains is due to Nagaev \cite{Nagaev}. Theorems \ref{t.ThLLT} and \ref{ThLLTArrays} on the inhomogeneous Markov case above are from \cite{Dolgopyat-Sarig-Book}. There is a related result by Merlev\'ede, M. Peligrad and C. Peligrad in \cite{Peligrad-LLT}. For a fuller historical account and further references, see \cite[\S 1.7]{Dolgopyat-Sarig-Book}. 

 The rate of convergence in the local limit theorem is discussed in
 \cite{Dolgopyat-Hafouta-iid, Dolgopyat-Hafouta-mc}.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- defi-18: body_md -->
\label{DefFreeEn}
 Suppose $V_N\neq 0$ for all $N\geq \nu_0$. \index{Log-moment generating function}
 The {\em log moment generating function} with parameter $N\geq \nu_0$ is the function   $\mathcal{F}_N:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ ($N\geq\nu_0$) given by 
$$ \mathcal{F}_N(\xi)=\frac{1}{V_N} \log{\mathbb{E}}\left(e^{\xi S_N}\right).$$
<!-- end defi-18 -->
<!-- prop-16: body_md -->
\label{PrFreeEn}
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain $\mathsf X$, such that $V_N>0$ for all $N\geq \nu_0$. Then for all $N\geq\nu_0$, 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  $\mathcal{F}_N(0)=0$,    $\displaystyle \mathcal{F}_N'(0)=\frac{{\mathbb{E}}(S_N)}{V_N}$ and $\mathcal{F}_N''(0)=1.$
\item  $\mathcal{F}_N$ is real-analytic and  strictly convex on $\mathbb R$. Moreover,  given $R>0$ there is a constant
$c_R\!\!>\!\!0$ such that  $\displaystyle  c_R\leq \mathcal{F}_N''\leq c_R^{-1}\textrm{ on $[-R, R]$ for all $N\geq \nu_0$.}$
\item Suppose $V_N\to\infty$. For every ${\varepsilon}>0$ there are $\delta, N_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that for all $|\xi|\leq \delta$ and $N>N_{\varepsilon}$, we have 
$e^{-{\varepsilon}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\xi^2\leq \mathcal{F}_N(\xi)-\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\xi\leq e^{+{\varepsilon}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\xi^2$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-16 -->
<!-- defi-19: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional\index{Log-moment generating function!Legendre transform}\index{Rate function} on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain $\mathsf X$, and $V_N>0$ for all $N\geq \nu_0$. 
The {\em rate function} with parameter $N\geq \nu_0$ is the Legendre transform of $\mathcal{F}_N$, namely $\mathcal{I}_N:(a_N^\infty,b_N^\infty)\to\mathbb R$ given by 
$$
\mathcal{I}_N(\eta):=\xi\eta-\mathcal{F}_N(\xi)\textrm{ for the unique $\xi\in\mathbb R$ such that $\mathcal{F}_N'(\xi)=\eta$}.
$$
<!-- end defi-19 -->
<!-- prop-17: body_md -->
\label{PrRateFn}
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain $\mathsf X$, such that $V_N>0$ for all $N\geq \nu_0$. Then
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item $\exists c,\nu_1,R>0$ such that for all $N>\nu_1$,
$$
\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{I}_N)\supset [a_N^R,b_N^R]\supset\left[\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}-c,\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}+c \right].
$$
\item For each $R$ there exists $\rho=\rho(R)>0$ such that for all $N>\nu_1$, 
$$
\rho^{-1}\leq \mathcal{I}_N''\leq\rho\textrm{ on }[a_N^R,b_N^R].
$$
\item Suppose $V_N\to\infty$. For every ${\varepsilon}>0$, there exists $\delta>0$ and $N_{\varepsilon}$ such that for all $\eta\in \left[\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}-\delta, \frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}+\delta\right]$ and $N>N_{\varepsilon}$, 
    $$
    e^{-{\varepsilon}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(\eta-\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right)^2\leq \mathcal{I}_N(\eta)\leq     e^{{\varepsilon}}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(\eta-\frac{\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right)^2.
    $$
\item Suppose $V_N\to\infty$ and $\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}0$, then 
$$
V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)=\frac{1+o(1)}{2}
\left(\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N}}\right)^2\textrm{, as $N\to\infty$.}
$$  
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-17 -->
<!-- thm-38: body_md -->
\label{t.LDP}
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain such that  $V_N\to\infty$. For every ${\varepsilon},R>0$, there are constants $D, \nu_2>0$   such that for all $N>\nu_2$:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  If $\frac{z_N}{V_N}\in [\mathcal{F}_N'({\varepsilon}), \mathcal{F}_N'(R)]$, then 
$$
\frac{D^{-1}}{\sqrt{V_N}}e^{-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)}\leq {\mathbb{P}}(S_N\geq z_N)\leq 
\frac{D}{\sqrt{V_N}}e^{-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)};
$$

\item  If $\frac{z_N}{V_N}\in [\mathcal{F}_N'(-R),\mathcal{F}_N'(-{\varepsilon})]$, then 
$$
\frac{D^{-1}}{\sqrt{V_N}}e^{-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)}\leq {\mathbb{P}}(S_N\leq z_N)\leq 
\frac{D}{\sqrt{V_N}}e^{-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)}.
$$
\end{enumerate}
Moreover,  $D$ can be chosen to depend only on ${\varepsilon}$, $R$, and 
$\displaystyle K:=\sup_n\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f_n(X_n,X_{n+1})|$.
<!-- end thm-38 -->
<!-- thm-39: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf f$ be an irreducible, uniformly bounded,  additive functional with algebraic range $\mathbb Z$, on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain $\mathsf X$. For every sequence of integers $z_N$ such that $\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\to 0$, 
\begin{align*}
{\mathbb{P}}[S_N=z_N]&=\frac{1+o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi V_N}}\exp\left[-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)\right]\\
&=\frac{1+o(1)}{\sqrt{2\pi V_N}}\exp\left[-\frac{1+o(1)}{2}\left(\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{\sqrt{V_N}}\right)^2\right].
\end{align*}
<!-- end thm-39 -->
<!-- defi-20: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathsf f$ is a uniformly bounded additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain, such that $V_N\to\infty$.  
A sequence of numbers $\{z_N\}$  is called  {\em admissible} for $(\mathsf X, \mathsf f)$,  if there exists $R$ such that 
$\frac{z_N}{V_N} \in [a_N^R, b_N^R]$ for all $N$ large.\index{Admissible large deviations regime}
<!-- end defi-20 -->
<!-- thm-40: body_md -->
\label{ThLD}
Let $\mathsf f$ be an integer-valued uniformly bounded additive functional on a uniformly elliptic Markov chain $\mathsf X$. Suppose $(\mathsf X,\mathsf f)$ is irreducible  with algebraic range $\mathbb Z$.  Then there are positive functions $\rho_N(\cdot)$ as follows:\index{Large deviations bounds!LLT for admissible large deviations}\index{Local limit theorem!for admissible large deviations}
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item  For every admissible  sequence of integers $z_N$, 
$$
{\mathbb{P}}[S_N=z_N]=[1+o(1)]\frac{e^{-V_N\mathcal{I}_N\left(\frac{z_N}{V_N}\right)}}{\sqrt{2\pi V_N}}\times\rho_N\left(\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right), \textrm{ as $N\to\infty$}.
$$
\item $\rho_N(\eta)\xrightarrow[\eta\to 0]{}1$ uniformly in $N$, and  $\forall R>0$, $\exists c_R>1$ such that for $N$ and $z_N$ such that $\frac{z_N}{V_N}\in [a_N^R,b_N^R]$, 
$
c_R^{-1}\leq \rho_N\left(\frac{z-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right)\leq c_R.
$
\item In particular, if $z_N$ is admissible, then $\rho_N\left(\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right)\asymp 1$, and if $\frac{z-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\to 0$, then $\rho_N\left(\frac{z_N-\mathbb E(S_N)}{V_N}\right)\to 1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end thm-40 -->
